KCS
Your first choice: KKR Global Client Solutions, London.
6 Jun to 29 Jul
The 2027 internship, eight weeks in the London office.

No interview is scheduled yet, and the interviewers are not known. The ten-minute emergency version@@k0-ten@@

If you read nothing else, read these ten points. Each is expanded, with sources, later in the pack.

  1. What KKR is. A listed alternative asset manager: it invests clients' money in private equity, private credit, infrastructure and real estate, and owns an insurer, Global Atlantic. $796.5bn of assets under management at 30 June 2026 [S1] CONFIRMED.
  2. Who pays KKR. Its clients (limited partners): pensions, sovereign wealth funds, insurers, endowments, family offices and, increasingly, wealthy individuals. They pay management fees and a share of profits (carried interest).
  3. What KCS is. The team that raises and looks after that money: formed in 2009, 300+ people, split into relationship management and product/strategy management [S103, S141] CONFIRMED. KKR's words: it exists to "connect the dots" across all of KKR's businesses [S141].
  4. The three client channels. Institutions, Family Capital and Global Wealth. Private wealth is now 18% of KKR's AUM, ahead of pensions at 14% [S71] CONFIRMED. The wealth products are the evergreen K-Series, which grew from $6bn (2023) to $42bn (June 2026) [S72, S73].
  5. Why KCS works with Capital Markets. KKR can underwrite a deal and syndicate co-investment to clients through KCM; KCS brings the clients [S70]. In Europe one Partner, Mark Danzey, heads both KCM and Institutional Client Solutions [S156] CONFIRMED.
  6. Why KKR is built this way. One firm, one P&L, one compensation pool [S5]; employees own about 30% of the stock [S3]. So the client team can sell what fits the client, not what one team needs to fill INFERRED.
  7. The year so far. Record fundraising pace: $305bn raised since the start of 2024 against a $300bn target [S76]; Global Infrastructure Investors V closed at $19.2bn in August 2026, KKR's largest infrastructure fund [S176].
  8. The awkward facts. A proposed $250m DOJ settlement over merger filings (Aug 2026) [S205]; K-FIT paid about 80% of redemption requests in Q1 2026, then 100% in Q2 [S338]; founders' control ends by 31 Dec 2026 [S2]. Know them; state them neutrally.
  9. Where KKR does not lead. Blackstone and Apollo are larger, Blackstone leads private wealth by a wide margin, and in-house capital markets is not unique [S213, S215, S220]. Never overclaim.
  10. Your answer. "KCS is the team that has to understand all of KKR. KKR is built for that seat. I want to learn the whole firm by explaining it honestly to the people who fund it." Then one personal example of explaining something or keeping a commitment.

Part 1

Before anything: private markets from zero

Every assumption the job description takes for granted, explained from the ground up.

This part assumes you know nothing. By the end you should be able to draw, on a blank sheet, how money moves from a pension fund into a KKR fund, into companies and back again, who takes what along the way, and why the people who raise that money (KKR Global Client Solutions, "KCS") are having a busy 2026.

$796bn
KKR assets under management, 30 Jun 2026 [S330] CONFIRMED
$16.7tn
Private capital AUM worldwide, Dec 2025 (PitchBook) [S260] REPORTED
$133bn
New capital KKR raised in the 12 months to 30 Jun 2026 [S330] CONFIRMED

1. Investing, and what an "alternative" asset manager is@@b-what@@

Investing means handing over money today to get more back later. The person or institution with the money (a pension fund, an insurer, a wealthy family) usually does not pick the investments itself. It hires an asset manager and pays it a fee. The asset manager's product is a fund: a pot of money from many investors, run under one set of rules.

Key term

Traditional investments are listed shares (stocks), government and company bonds, and cash. You can buy and sell them every trading day at a public price INFERRED. Alternative investments are everything else that big investors buy: private equity, private credit, infrastructure, real estate, hedge funds and natural resources [S269] REPORTED. Their defining feature is that they are illiquid: you cannot sell them quickly at a known price. In return investors hope for an illiquidity premium, a higher return than public markets INFERRED.

Five kinds of firm get confused all the time. Here is the difference in one line each [Inferred, standard definitions]:

  • Traditional asset manager (BlackRock, Vanguard): mostly index funds and listed share and bond funds. Very low fees, huge scale, daily liquidity.
  • Hedge fund: trades mostly liquid securities, often with monthly or quarterly liquidity, and aims for returns that do not move with the market.
  • Investment bank: advises on deals (mergers, listings) and underwrites securities. Paid per transaction, not a long-term management fee. Banks are counterparties and lenders to the firms above.
  • Private equity firm: buys whole companies that are not on the stock market, improves them and sells them, using funds that last about ten years.
  • Alternative asset manager (KKR, Blackstone, Apollo, Carlyle, Ares, Brookfield, EQT): a private equity firm that grew into many strategies. Runs long-lived private funds, earns management fees plus a share of profits, and increasingly owns insurance companies and runs products for individuals.

KKR is the clearest example of that growth. At 31 December 2010 traditional private equity was over 70% of KKR's assets under management. At 30 June 2026 it was "less than 25%" [S332] CONFIRMED. Today KKR's $796bn splits into Credit and Liquid Strategies $331bn, Real Assets $211bn and Private Equity $255bn [S332] CONFIRMED.

Say this in the interview

"KKR started as a buyout firm but is now mostly a credit, infrastructure and insurance business. Private equity is less than a quarter of its assets. So KCS is not selling one product, it is selling a platform."

2. The GP / LP structure: who gives what, who gets what@@b-gplp@@

A private fund is usually set up as a limited partnership, a legal form with two kinds of partner INFERRED.

Key term

General partner (GP): the manager. KKR, Blackstone, Apollo and Carlyle act as GPs. The GP picks the investments, runs them and decides when to sell INFERRED. It also puts in some of its own money, the GP commitment, so it has "skin in the game" INFERRED.

Key term

Limited partners (LPs): the investors who supply most of the money. "Limited" because they cannot lose more than they put in and they do not run the fund INFERRED. Pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurers, endowments, family offices and wealthy individuals.

The contract between them is the limited partnership agreement (LPA). Individual LPs often negotiate extra terms in a side letter, for example a fee discount or extra reporting INFERRED. The LPs' trade body, ILPA (Institutional Limited Partners Association), lists three guiding principles: alignment of interest, governance and transparency [S317] CONFIRMED. Keep those three words in your head: they are what every LP is checking when it meets KCS.

PartyGivesGets
LPA commitment (a legal promise to pay up to a set amount when asked); cash when called; patience for about 10 yearsMost of the profits; access to deals it could not do alone; quarterly reports; a say on conflicts (through an advisory committee)
GPDeal-finding, management, operating help; its own GP commitment; a track recordA management fee every year; carried interest (a share of profits above a hurdle); the platform to raise the next fund

The next page draws the whole system on one sheet. Learn to sketch it from memory. It is the single most useful drawing for a fundraising interview.

3. The life of a closed-end (drawdown) fund@@b-life@@

Most KKR flagship funds are closed-end: investors join only during fundraising, then the door shuts and the fund runs for a fixed life. They are also called drawdown funds, because the GP "draws down" committed money in stages. Think of it as a ten-year journey in four stages [Inferred, standard model]:

  1. Fundraising and commitment. The GP markets the fund. LPs sign a commitment to give, say, $100m when asked. No cash moves yet. The fund holds a first close (the first date it accepts commitments and can start investing) and later a final close (the last day it accepts new investors) INFERRED.
  2. Investment period (roughly years 1 to 5). When the GP finds a deal it sends a capital call (also called a drawdown) asking each LP for its share. LPs must pay within days. Money promised but not yet called is dry powder or unfunded commitments INFERRED.
  3. Value creation and harvest (roughly years 4 to 10). The GP improves the companies, then sells them in an exit: a sale to another company, a sale to another fund, or a stock market listing (IPO) INFERRED.
  4. Distribution. Cash from exits goes back to LPs. The fund usually has a 10-year life, often with 1 to 2 years of extensions INFERRED.

A real example: in April 2026 KKR held the final close of North America Fund XIV at about $23bn, which KKR calls the largest private equity fund focused only on North America [S335] CONFIRMED. Its LPs included public and private pension plans, sovereign wealth funds, insurers, endowments and foundations, private wealth platforms, family offices and wealthy individuals [S335] REPORTED. That list is the KCS client map.

The J-curve: why the early years look bad

Plot an LP's cumulative net cash flow (all cash received minus all cash paid in) over the fund's life. In the early years the LP pays capital calls and fees but gets little back, so the line falls. Once exits start, it climbs. The shape looks like a letter J INFERRED. The bottom of the J is where LPs feel the most strain, and it is why slow exits in 2022 to 2026 hurt so much.

Why this matters

Exits have been slow, so the J has been stuck near the bottom for many funds. PitchBook counts almost $5tn sitting in funds that are seven years old or older, 39% of total NAV, as of December 2025 [S260] REPORTED. Bain counts about 32,000 unsold portfolio companies worth about $3.8tn [S262, S326] CONFIRMED. LPs with no cash coming back have less to commit to the next fund. That is the KCS problem in one sentence.

4. Fees and the waterfall@@b-fees@@

The industry shorthand is "2 and 20". The real terms vary by fund, and large LPs often negotiate lower ones [Inferred, standard definitions].

Key terms

Management fee (the "2"): about 1.5% to 2% a year of committed capital during the investment period, often stepping down later to invested capital. Pays salaries and running costs INFERRED.

Carried interest or "carry" (the "20"): the GP's share of profits, typically 20% INFERRED.

Hurdle rate or preferred return: the minimum return LPs must earn before the GP gets any carry, commonly 8% a year INFERRED.

Catch-up: once the hurdle is cleared, the GP takes a large share of the next profits until it has "caught up" to 20% of total profit INFERRED.

Waterfall: the order in which cash is paid out. A European (whole-of-fund) waterfall pays carry only after LPs get all their money back plus the hurdle across the whole fund. An American (deal-by-deal) waterfall can pay carry deal by deal, which is better for the GP INFERRED. A clawback makes the GP repay carry if later losses mean it was overpaid; ILPA's Principles 2.0 (2011) added a clawback appendix [S317] CONFIRMED.

Worked example you can do on paper

All numbers are illustrative. A fund has $100m paid in by LPs. After exactly five years every investment has been sold for $200m in total. The terms: 8% preferred return (simple, not compounded, to keep the maths easy; real funds usually compound), 100% GP catch-up, 20% carry, European waterfall. Ignore fees inside the example.

StepRuleMathsTo LPsTo GPLeft in the pot
StartTotal exit proceeds$200m
1 Return of capitalLPs get their $100m back first100$100m0$100m
2 Preferred return8% a year for 5 years on $100m100 x 8% x 5 = 40$40m0$60m
3 Catch-upGP takes 100% until it has 20% of all profit paid so farC = 20% x (40 + C), so C = 100$10m$50m
4 SplitRemainder 80 / 2050 x 80% ; 50 x 20%$40m$10m0
Total$180m$20m

Check: total profit is $100m and the GP got $20m, exactly 20%. The LPs turned $100m into $180m, so their net multiple is 1.8x even though the fund's gross multiple was 2.0x. That gap (plus fees, which we ignored) is why LPs always ask whether a figure is gross or net.

Now add the management fee. At 2% a year on $100m of commitments for a five-year investment period, the GP would collect $10m of fees before any carry (illustrative). The fee is paid whether or not the fund makes money. Carry is paid only if it does. That is why LPs like a large GP commitment: if the GP has its own money in the fund, it suffers losses alongside them.

Don't say this

"KKR makes its money from carried interest." Carry matters, but the steady engine is fees. KKR's Fee Related Earnings were $1.2bn in Q2 2026 alone [S330] CONFIRMED, and its fee-paying AUM was $638bn [S330] CONFIRMED. Say: "Fees pay for the platform; carry rewards performance."

5. Performance metrics: IRR, MOIC, TVPI, DPI, RVPI, PME@@b-metrics@@

LPs judge a GP by its numbers. Six abbreviations do most of the work [Inferred, standard definitions]:

MetricPlain EnglishFormula
IRR internal rate of returnThe annualised return, taking timing into account. Returning money fast boosts IRR.The yearly rate that makes all cash in and out net to zero
MOIC multiple on invested capitalHow many times your money you got back. $1 in, $2.50 out = 2.5x.Total value / amount invested
TVPI total value to paid-inThe LP-level version of MOIC: cash already back plus what is still held.(Distributions + remaining value) / paid-in
DPI distributions to paid-inCash actually returned. "Real money."Distributions / paid-in
RVPI residual value to paid-inValue still sitting in the fund, on paper.Remaining value (NAV) / paid-in
PME public market equivalentDid the fund beat what the same cash flows would have earned in a stock index?Fund result compared with an index on matched cash flows

The one equation to remember is TVPI = DPI + RVPI. NAV (net asset value) is the GP's own estimate of what the unsold holdings are worth, updated quarterly.

Mini-example (illustrative numbers)

An LP has paid in $50m. By year 6 it has received $30m in cash and the holdings left are valued at $55m. DPI = 30 / 50 = 0.6x. RVPI = 55 / 50 = 1.1x. TVPI = 0.6 + 1.1 = 1.7x. The fund looks good on paper, but only 0.6x is cash in hand.

Why IRR is not enough. Fund A doubles money (2.0x) in 3 years: IRR is about 26% a year, since 2 to the power of one-third is about 1.26. Fund B doubles money in 8 years: IRR is about 9%, since 2 to the power of one-eighth is about 1.09. Same multiple, very different experience. Always quote a multiple and an IRR together.

Why DPI is the word of 2025-26

If exits are slow, a fund can show a fine TVPI while sending back little cash. LPs need cash to pay pensions and to fund new commitments, so they now ask about DPI first INFERRED. The evidence:

  • Bain: distributions as a share of NAV were about 14% in 2025, and below 15% for four years running [S262] CONFIRMED.
  • McKinsey's 2026 report (via a Dakota summary): distributions fell to 6% of AUM against a 2015 to 2019 average of 16% [S261] REPORTED.
  • Bain cites an ILPA survey in which 53% of LPs said undrawn commitments limit new private equity commitments, up 15 percentage points [S262] CONFIRMED.
Source uncertain

Bain's 2025 report described 2024 distributions as the lowest rate in over a decade (one reprint says 11%), which does not square neatly with "essentially flat at 14%" in the 2026 report [S271] REPORTED. Quote the provider with the number, and say "about".

KKR leans into this. Its co-CEOs called Q2 2026 KKR's "strongest monetization quarter ever" (monetisation means selling or part-selling investments and returning cash) [S330] CONFIRMED. In August 2026 Aon agreed to buy USI Insurance Services from KKR and co-investors for about $17bn including debt, reported at about 6x KKR's original equity [S354] REPORTED. Exits like that are the best fundraising argument there is.

Say this in the interview

"TVPI tells you what a fund might be worth. DPI tells you what an LP can actually spend. After four years of distributions under 15% of NAV, DPI is what gets a pension fund to re-up."

6. The asset classes KKR's internship teams invest in@@b-assets@@

Candidates for the London internship rank six teams: Private Equity (including Global Impact), Real Estate, Infrastructure, Capital Markets, Client Solutions and Capstone. KCS has to explain all of the investing strategies to clients. KCS itself says it "connect[s] the dots" across Private Equity, Infrastructure, Real Estate, Credit, Capital Markets and Insurance-Funded Strategies [S390] CONFIRMED.

KKR-specific markers: Global Infrastructure Investors V closed at $19.2bn in August 2026, KKR's largest infrastructure fund [S334] CONFIRMED; KKR's alternative credit includes $91bn of asset-based finance and $48bn of corporate private credit, of which $39bn is direct lending [S332] CONFIRMED.

7. Who the LPs are, and what each one needs@@b-lps@@

KCS's clients are LPs. Each type has different liabilities (what it owes in future), a different horizon (how long it can wait), different liquidity needs (how fast it may need cash back) and a different ticket size (how much it commits per fund). The descriptions below are the standard picture INFERRED; the research found no 2026 breakdown of how much each type holds.

Key term

Defined benefit (DB) pension: the employer promises a set income in retirement (say, a share of final salary), so the fund has fixed long-term liabilities and the employer carries the investment risk. Defined contribution (DC) pension: the employer and worker pay into a personal pot; the retirement income depends on how the pot performs, so the saver carries the risk. DC funds need daily pricing and switching, which makes illiquid funds harder to hold INFERRED. UK change: 17 workplace pension providers, covering about 90% of active DC savers, pledged in the Mansion House Accord (13 May 2025) to put at least 10% of DC default funds in private markets by 2030, with at least 5% in the UK [S315] CONFIRMED.

  • Pensions are historically the largest LP group INFERRED. Many are now over-allocated: S&P Global found 174 of 298 pension funds analysed were over their private equity target in Q1 2025 [S324] REPORTED. In the UK, the Local Government Pension Scheme holds over £400bn across 86 funds and is consolidating into six pools [S347] REPORTED: fewer, bigger clients.
  • Insurers are growing fast as LPs because they want long-dated credit INFERRED. KKR owns one: Global Atlantic had $220bn of AUM at 30 June 2026 [S330] CONFIRMED.
  • Private wealth is the big gap. Bain estimates individuals hold about 50% of global AUM ($275tn to $295tn) but only 16% of AUM held by alternative funds [S293] REPORTED. PitchBook: "Growing inflows from retail investors are becoming the main source of new capital" [S260] CONFIRMED.
Source uncertain

No 2026 figure was found for the share of global private capital held by each LP type, and no sourced ticket sizes. Do not quote percentages for "pensions are X% of LPs".

8. Evergreen (semi-liquid) funds versus drawdown funds@@b-evergreen@@

A wealthy individual cannot easily handle ten years of unpredictable capital calls. So managers built a second kind of vehicle.

Key term

Evergreen or semi-liquid fund: a fund with no fixed end date. Investors subscribe (buy in) monthly at the latest NAV per share, and can ask to redeem (cash out), usually quarterly, up to a cap, often 5% of the fund per quarter [S278] REPORTED. When requests exceed the cap, a gate applies and requests are paid pro rata (everyone gets the same fraction). Examples: non-traded BDCs (US private credit vehicles), non-traded REITs, ELTIFs in Europe, LTAFs in the UK INFERRED.

Why this is the private wealth channel's vehicle

  • Size: semi-liquid evergreen vehicles hold about $500bn of industry AUM (Evercore) [S267] REPORTED. US evergreen PE AUM nearly doubled from $51.3bn (end-2024) to $99.3bn (Q1 2026), which "funnels more capital into the hands of the largest GPs with established wealth products" (PitchBook) [S260] REPORTED.
  • KKR's version is K-Series, its family of funds for wealthy individuals sold through banks and advisers. K-Series AUM was $42bn at 30 June 2026, up from $25bn a year earlier [S330, S332] CONFIRMED.
  • The stress test: in Q1 2026 wealthy investors asked to withdraw $20.8bn from private credit funds run by Apollo, Ares, Blackstone, Blue Owl, KKR and others; managers paid "just over half" of requests [S337] REPORTED. Blue Owl enforced a 5% quarterly cap on 2 April 2026 [S278] REPORTED. Blackstone's BCRED paid 100% of record requests of 7.9% of NAV [S278] REPORTED. KKR's K-FIT received requests for 6.3% of shares in Q1 and paid about 80% of them; in Q2 requests fell to 1.65% and were paid in full [S338] REPORTED.
  • Europe and the UK have their own wrappers: 189 new ELTIFs since start-2024 and about €34bn of ELTIF assets at end-2025 [S302] REPORTED; the UK LTAF was opened to retail investors from 3 July 2023 [S305] CONFIRMED.
Your opinion goes here

Was Q1 2026 a failure of semi-liquid funds, or proof that gates work as designed? One defensible line: "The gates did their job. The lesson for a client team is to set liquidity expectations when the fund is sold, not when the queue forms." Decide whether you agree and why.

9. Secondaries, continuation vehicles, co-investment, SMAs and the denominator effect@@b-liquidity@@

These five ideas all answer one LP question: "How do I get the exposure I want, on terms I like, without being stuck?"

Key term

LP-led secondary: an LP sells its stake in a fund to a specialist buyer, usually at a price near NAV, to get cash early INFERRED.

Key term

GP-led secondary / continuation vehicle (CV): the GP moves one or more prized assets from an old fund into a new vehicle. Old LPs can cash out or roll over; new investors come in INFERRED.

Bain found CV transaction value grew 62% in 2025, but CVs were still less than 10% of exit value [S262] CONFIRMED. Evercore calls secondaries' shift "from an episodic liquidity solution into a structural portfolio management channel" [S267] CONFIRMED. KKR bought Arctos Partners (closed 4 May 2026); its team now forms "KKR Solutions", which KKR says will house "a scaled multi-asset class secondaries business" [S330, S332] CONFIRMED [S355] REPORTED.

Key term

Co-investment: an LP invests directly in one deal alongside the fund, usually with no or low fees [S260] CONFIRMED. It lowers the LP's average fee and lets the GP do a bigger deal. PitchBook tracks $37.5bn of co-investment fundraising in the 12 months to June 2026 [S260] CONFIRMED.

Key term

Separately managed account (SMA): instead of joining a pooled fund, one large LP gets its own account run by the GP, with terms, strategy mix and reporting built for it INFERRED. This is what "customized products" in the KCS job description points at INFERRED.

The denominator effect

Pension funds set a target allocation, for example "15% in private equity". When listed markets fall fast (as in 2022), the value of the listed shares drops at once, but private holdings are revalued only quarterly and more slowly. Private assets become a bigger share of the total even though nothing was bought. The fund may then be "over-allocated" and stop making new commitments [S323] REPORTED.

This was not just a 2022 story. S&P Global found 174 of 298 pension funds analysed over-allocated to private equity in Q1 2025 [S324] REPORTED, and PitchBook says institutional allocations are "bumping up against risk limits" [S260] REPORTED. Secondaries are one way out: an over-allocated LP can sell stakes to get back under target.

10. How big the industry is, and the fundraising market today@@b-market@@

Source uncertain: read this before quoting any number

Every data provider (PitchBook, Preqin, Bain, McKinsey) defines "private markets" and "fundraising" differently. Some count venture capital, some do not; some count only closed-end funds. The totals do not add up to each other. Always quote the provider and the scope together. McKinsey's own reports could not be read in full; only summaries were used [S264] REPORTED.

$6.1tn → $16.7tn
Private capital AUM, 2016 to Dec 2025 (PitchBook) [S260] REPORTED
~$32tn
Alternatives AUM forecast for 2030 (Preqin, Oct 2025; wider scope incl. hedge funds) [S269] CONFIRMED
$2.35tn
PE dry powder, 25% of AUM, Q4 2025 (Preqin) [S266] REPORTED

The fundraising story, year by year

  • 2024: fundraising fell around 23% to 24% across private market asset classes; Bain blamed the "persistent liquidity situation" for LPs [S271] REPORTED. McKinsey called it the lowest level since 2016 [S264] REPORTED.
  • 2025: Bain counts about $1.3tn raised in total, about flat, with buyout down 16% to $395bn, a fourth straight annual decline; growth came from infrastructure and secondaries [S262] CONFIRMED. Preqin: PE excluding VC $660.7bn, down 9%, with funds closed down 26% to 1,205 [S265] CONFIRMED. Cambridge Associates: fundraising "troughed in 2025 at roughly one-third of 2021 levels" [S261] REPORTED.
  • 2026 to 30 June: PitchBook counts $658.1bn across 1,499 funds in H1, with the 12-month total down 12.7% and fund count down 37%; if the pace holds, 2026 is the fifth straight annual decline [S260] CONFIRMED. But for the biggest firms it is a rebound: average time to close fell to 15.7 months and 82% of PE funds closed at or above target, the highest in at least six years [S266] CONFIRMED. And 7,739 PE funds are on the road, the most in five years [S266] CONFIRMED. KKR raised $34bn in Q2 2026 and expects "a record fundraising year for the firm" [S330] CONFIRMED [S362] REPORTED.

More signs of the flight to scale: in PE, 77% of capital since 2024 went to funds over $1bn; only 36 first-time PE funds closed in H1 2026, raising $7.7bn [S260] CONFIRMED. The ten largest funds closed in Q2 2026 took 49% of the quarter's capital [S266] CONFIRMED. PitchBook reads this as allocators "gravitating toward GPs with established track records and broad market validation rather than expending the resources required to underwrite smaller, less-proven vehicles" [S260] CONFIRMED. Bain: "Investors more than ever are focused on funds that have a clear, repeatable, and easily explained strategy" [S262] CONFIRMED.

11. The structural forces reshaping the industry now@@b-forces@@

Six forces matter most for someone joining a fundraising team in 2027. The map below puts each one next to its best data point and what it means for KCS.

What sits behind each force

  • Wealth. Executive Order 14330 (7 August 2025) told the US Department of Labor to re-examine 401(k) guidance [S273] CONFIRMED; the DOL proposed a process-based safe harbour on 30 March 2026, with no final rule found as of 11 October 2026 [S272, S274] CONFIRMED. Around 30 September 2026 the SEC proposed widening the "accredited investor" test beyond income and wealth, adding an exam and professional routes such as the CFA charter [S275] REPORTED. Bain projects private wealth allocations to alternatives could grow from about $4tn (2022) to over $13tn by 2032 [S293] REPORTED. KKR and Capital Group announced plans in December 2025 that include a target-date fund for 401(k) plans [S363] REPORTED.
  • Insurance and credit. Large managers own or partner with life insurers (Apollo with Athene, KKR with Global Atlantic). The insurer collects premiums and invests them in long-dated private credit the manager originates [S285] REPORTED. Apollo argues private credit is a market "of over $40 trillion", mostly investment grade [S285] REPORTED; critics say "private credit" as most people mean it is about $1.7tn to $3tn [S286] REPORTED.
  • Credit stress. Tricolor filed for Chapter 7 on 10 September 2025 [S282] REPORTED; First Brands filed for Chapter 11 around 28 September 2025 with liabilities over $10bn [S283] REPORTED. Jamie Dimon: "when you see one cockroach, there are probably more" [S280] CONFIRMED. BlueBay's Mark Dowding called Tricolor "corporate fraud rather than an underlying symptom of credit market conditions" [S281] REPORTED. Contrast: closed-end private debt funds had a record 2025 net cash flow of $39.5bn, behaving "differently from evergreen vehicles" [S260] REPORTED.
  • AI. Meta and Blue Owl's Hyperion data-centre joint venture issued $27bn of bonds, described as the largest private credit deal ever [S289] REPORTED. Redemption requests at Blue Owl's BDCs were partly driven by AI disruption risk to software borrowers [S279] REPORTED.
  • Consolidation. BlackRock's GIP and HPS deals were "the two largest-ever acquisitions of alternative asset managers in less than a year" [S290] REPORTED. Morgan Stanley and Oliver Wyman forecast more than 1,500 asset manager M&A deals through 2029 [S291] REPORTED.

Where the industry goes in 3 to 5 years: four competing views

Your opinion goes here

Pick one view and one piece of evidence that would change your mind. Example structure: "I lean to view 2 for the industry but view 1 for the largest firms, because 78.2% of capital already goes to $1bn+ funds [S260]. I would change my mind if evergreen redemptions stayed above the 5% gates for several more quarters." Write your own version and practise it aloud in 45 seconds.

12. What this means for a fundraising role@@b-role@@

  • The market shrinks, the leaders grow. Buyout fundraising fell for a fourth straight year in 2025 and PitchBook sees 2026 as a fifth straight annual decline for private capital overall [S262, S260], yet KKR raised $133bn in 12 months [S330]. KCS is where share is won INFERRED.
  • DPI is the opening question. LPs short of distributions ask about cash returned before anything else. Exits like USI are the evidence KCS uses [S354] REPORTED.
  • Two client worlds. Institutions buy drawdown funds, SMAs and co-investments; individuals buy evergreen funds through banks and advisers. KCS covers both, with different languages for each [S388, S390] CONFIRMED.
  • Liquidity is now part of the pitch. Gates, pro-rating, secondaries and CVs are basic vocabulary after Q1 2026 [S337, S338] REPORTED.
  • Fewer, bigger buyers. UK LGPS pools and £25bn+ DC megafunds want customised, fee-efficient access [S346, S347], which is the "customized products" line in the KCS description INFERRED.
  • Platform, not product. KCS "connect[s] the dots" from PE to infrastructure, real estate, credit, capital markets and insurance [S390] CONFIRMED. Knowing all six asset classes in this part is the entry ticket.
  • Trust is the currency. KKR's own line: "People do business with people they like and trust" [S384] CONFIRMED. Every number you give a client must be one you can source.
Say this in the interview

"Industry fundraising has fallen for several years, but capital is concentrating in large platforms: funds over $1bn took 78% of the money in the first half of 2026. LPs are short of distributions, so the conversation now starts with DPI and liquidity. That makes Client Solutions more important, not less: the team has to explain everything from a drawdown buyout fund to a semi-liquid credit fund, to a pension and to a wealth adviser, in their own language."

Don't say this

"Private equity is booming and everyone wants in." It is wrong on the data (buyout fundraising fell for a fourth straight year in 2025 [S262]), it ignores the 2026 redemption queues, and it tells the interviewer you have read headlines, not numbers. Also avoid quoting one total for "the industry" without naming the provider and scope.

@@k2@@
Part 2

KKR from the inside

How the firm makes money, how it is governed, what it promises its clients and what has gone wrong. The product you would be selling.

A. The founding insight: three people, a borrowed-money idea, and a firm built around it@@f-founding@@

KKR began as an idea that a big Wall Street bank refused to back. Almost everything about how KKR is built today (who owns it, how people are paid, how long client money is locked in) traces back to that idea and to the partnership of the three men who had it.

Bear Stearns and the "bootstrap" deals

Jerome Kohlberg Jr. ran corporate finance at the investment bank Bear, Stearns & Co. His two protégés were first cousins: Henry Kravis and George Roberts [S27, S28] CONFIRMED. From the mid 1960s the three did what they called "bootstrap" acquisitions. They bought mostly family-owned companies using a small slice of their own money (equity) and a lot of borrowed money (debt) [S27, S28] CONFIRMED. A reference history credits Kohlberg with first using the technique in 1965 [S27] REPORTED.

Key term

Leveraged buyout (LBO): buying a company mainly with borrowed money, where the debt is repaid from the company's own cash flows. The buyer improves the business, pays down the debt, then sells. Because the buyer put in only a small amount of equity, a modest rise in the company's value can multiply that equity many times. The "bootstrap" deals were the first version of this [S27, S28] CONFIRMED. (Fees, carry and fund mechanics are in the basics section; this part only uses them.)

The early results were mixed, which is worth knowing. Roberts and Kravis completed 14 buyouts between 1969 and 1975 with what one history calls "generally mediocre results" [S27] REPORTED. Some were spectacular: investors in Vapor Corp. (1972, about $37m) got 12 times their stake back when it was sold in 1978, and a Rockwell division bought in 1975 returned 22 times in five years. Others failed: Cobblers Industries (1971) went bankrupt [S27, S28] REPORTED. When Bear Stearns leadership refused to set up an in-house buyout fund, the three left to do it themselves [S28] REPORTED.

1 May 1976: "3 guys and a broom"

In KKR's own words: "On May 1, 1976, Henry Kravis and George Roberts co-founded KKR alongside their mentor Jerome Kohlberg with $120,000, launching what we now know as the alternatives industry" [S13] CONFIRMED. KKR describes the early firm as "3 guys and a broom" [S14] CONFIRMED. Its first buyout as KKR was A.J. Industries in 1976 [S28] REPORTED.

The first fund still appears in KKR's 2025 annual report. The "1976 Fund" took $31m of commitments and returned $537m: a 35.5% net IRR (the yearly return to investors after fees) and 17.1 times the money invested [S2] CONFIRMED. That track record is the reason pension funds later trusted three people with billions.

$120,000
Starting capital, 1 May 1976 [S13]
17.1x
Money multiple on the 1976 Fund ($31m in, $537m out) [S2]
50 years
Anniversary celebrated 1 May 2026 [S5, S13]

Scale, fame and the first break-up

The firm grew fast. Houdaille Industries (1979, about $355m) was then the largest LBO ever and KKR's first buyout of a major public company. Beatrice (1986, about $6.2bn) was financed partly with $2.5bn of "junk bonds" (high-interest, lower-rated bonds) arranged by Drexel [S27] REPORTED. In 1987 Kohlberg resigned, uneasy that KKR's deal hunting "disturbingly echoed the tactics of corporate raiders". He later sued over his reduced ownership; the case settled on undisclosed terms [S27, S28] REPORTED. Kravis and Roberts then ran the firm together as co-CEOs from 1987 until October 2021 [S10, S28] CONFIRMED. RJR Nabisco (1988 to 1989) made KKR famous and is covered straight in section I.

Source uncertain

You may read elsewhere that Capstone (KKR's operations team) dates from 2000 and KKR Capital Markets from 2007. Those dates were not confirmed in the research behind this pack. If you want to use them, check KKR's own history page first (kkr.com/about/history) [S13]. Safer line: "KKR added credit, capital markets, infrastructure and insurance over the 2000s and 2010s, and by 2025 traditional private equity was under a quarter of its money" [S2] CONFIRMED.

How the founding idea shaped KKR's design

You can draw a straight line from the 1976 idea to today's structure. This is the kind of link interviewers remember, because it shows you understand why the firm looks the way it does, not just what it does.

Mission and culture in KKR's own words@@f-culture@@

Interviewers test "fit" against a small set of phrases that KKR repeats everywhere. Learn the exact wording and the date. Then you can quote it accurately and say where you read it.

Exact wordsWho / whereDate and source

Two stories carry the culture better than any slogan. First, Kravis says his "best deal" was a company that went bankrupt: Walter Industries, bought in 1987. KKR spent almost 17 years and settled for over $300m (against $117m of KKR equity) to get fund investors their money back plus a small profit [S384] CONFIRMED. Second, he describes reprimanding an employee who "retraded" a loan deal with a bank in KKR's favour, and apologising to the bank's chief executive [S384] CONFIRMED. Both are about keeping promises to the people who trust you with money, which is the whole job of a client team.

Say this in the interview

"What struck me in Henry Kravis's 2024 pieces on culture was the Walter Industries story: 17 years spent getting investors their money back from a bankruptcy. For a client team that is the culture in one example. The product is trust, and KKR treats a promise to an LP as something you keep even when the deal goes wrong." [S384]

Source uncertain: "industrialist vision"

The phrase "industrialist vision" appears in the SEO London listing for this internship. Our research did not find it in any KKR document we read: the 10-K, the earnings releases, or kkr.com's About and History pages [S2, S12, S13]. Do not quote it as KKR's own wording. If you want to use the idea, attribute it: "the SEO listing describes KKR's industrialist vision", and then anchor it to something KKR does say, such as "supporting growth in its portfolio companies" [S1] or its ownership-culture programme [S387].

Don't say this

"KKR is a private equity firm." KKR describes itself as a global investment firm with asset management, insurance and strategic holdings [S1, S12]. Traditional private equity was under 25% of its money at the end of 2025 [S2] CONFIRMED. Also avoid generic praise ("prestigious", "market leader"). Use a number or a quote instead.

B. How KKR makes money now@@f-money@@

KKR reports three businesses, which it calls its "Three Engines of Growth" [S12] CONFIRMED. Each earns money in a different way. If you can explain the three engines and the "earnings ladder" in two minutes, you will be ahead of most candidates.

The earnings ladder, one rung at a time

KKR's earnings release builds profit up in steps. Each step has a name that analysts and KKR's own managers use on calls. You do not need the accounting, only the logic.

  • Fee Related Earnings (FRE): management fees, plus transaction and monitoring fees, plus fee-related performance revenues, minus the pay and costs tied to them. The steady, recurring profit of the asset manager [S1, S5] CONFIRMED.
  • Total Operating Earnings (TOE): FRE plus Insurance Operating Earnings plus Strategic Holdings Operating Earnings. KKR calls this "the more durable and recurring portion" of earnings. Introduced in November 2023 [S1, S11] CONFIRMED.
  • Total Investing Earnings: net realised performance income (carry after the staff share) plus net realised investment income (gains on KKR's own money) [S1] CONFIRMED.
  • Adjusted Net Income (ANI): TOE plus Total Investing Earnings, minus interest and taxes. KKR's headline "bottom line" [S1] CONFIRMED.
Why this matters

Investors pay more for steady earnings than for lumpy ones. That is why KKR keeps moving revenue into the "recurring" boxes. Example: from Q2 2026, performance fees from its K-Series private equity fund for wealthy individuals moved from carried interest (where 70% to 80% goes to staff) into fee-related performance revenues (where 15% to 20% does). CFO Rob Lewin said this "structurally increases" earnings per share [S1, S3] CONFIRMED. For a client team, this is the link: every dollar KCS raises into a fee-paying fund lands in the most valuable box. At 30 Jun 2026, $72bn of committed money was not yet paying fees, at an average of about 90 basis points (0.90%) [S1, S3] CONFIRMED. Simple maths: that is roughly $650m of yearly fees waiting to switch on once the money is invested (estimate, as of Jun 2026) INFERRED.

Fee rates in one paragraph

Management fees vary by product. Private equity drawdown funds charge 1.0% to 2.0% of commitments while investing, then 0.75% to 1.50% of invested capital; infrastructure and real estate 0.75% to 1.50%; CLOs 0.4% to 0.5%; open-ended vehicles 0.50% to 1.25% [S2] CONFIRMED. Carry is typically 10% to 20% of fund profits after a 6% to 8% preferred return [S2] CONFIRMED. Management fees were $4.1bn in 2025 and $4.6bn over the 12 months to Q2 2026, up 26% year on year in Q2 [S1] CONFIRMED. Realised carry was $1.88bn in 2025; $10.2bn of carry was earned on paper but not yet realised at 30 June 2026 [S1, S2] CONFIRMED.

The numbers over time

Say this in the interview

"KKR is really three businesses: an asset manager that earns steady fees, an insurer that earns a spread, and its own long-term holdings. About 84% of segment earnings over the last twelve months were the recurring kind. For a client solutions team that matters, because the money you raise turns into management fees, which feed Fee Related Earnings, which is the part of KKR the market values most." [S1, S3]

C. The contracts: who gives what, and who gets what@@f-contracts@@

A firm like KKR is a bundle of agreements with four groups: the clients who lend it their money (LPs), the people who work there, the shareholders who own the listed company, and KKR's own balance sheet. The trick is that the same people often sit in several groups at once. Employees own about 30% of the shares [S2, S3] CONFIRMED. Clients are sometimes shareholders too.

What LPs give and get

The fund mechanics are in the basics section. Here is what is specific to KKR. Fund lives vary by strategy: infrastructure and real estate drawdown funds invest for up to six years and last 10 to 13 years; credit drawdown funds last 8 to 10 years (up to 12); core private equity vehicles can last up to 25 years; open-ended vehicles have no end date [S2] CONFIRMED. Real examples from the June 2026 fund table: North America Fund XIV ($21.9bn committed at that date, investing April 2025 to April 2031), Global Infrastructure Investors V ($18.6bn, July 2024 to July 2030), European Fund VI ($7.5bn, June 2022 to June 2028) [S1] CONFIRMED. Both flagships later closed larger: about $23bn for North America XIV in April 2026 and $19.2bn for Infrastructure V in August 2026 [S334, S335] CONFIRMED.

Key term

Clawback: if a manager takes carry early in a fund's life and the fund later does worse, the manager must hand that carry back. KKR did exactly this in Q4 2025 on Asian Fund II: $344m repaid, $207m net after amounts recovered from current and former employees [S2, S4] CONFIRMED. It is the contract working as designed, and a good example to show you understand alignment.

What employees give and get

KKR pays from one compensation pool across the firm. The 10-K says pay "is based on the performance of KKR as a whole, in addition to an individual's contributions", and that KKR generally does not pay people "based solely on an individual's accomplishments in relation to the profits and losses" of one business [S2] CONFIRMED. Kravis says KKR has always worked this way, "creating a system in which we all succeed and fail together", and that everyone got "phantom equity" from the start [S385] CONFIRMED.

Carried interest from all funds is allocated to one vehicle, KKR Associates Holdings L.P., "the carry pool" [S2] CONFIRMED. The pay mix is base salary, a possible cash bonus, discretionary equity and, for select employees, a carry pool allocation [S2] CONFIRMED. On 29 November 2023 KKR made pay "more success based": more from carry, less from fees [S11] CONFIRMED. Bloomberg reported the shift: the staff share of carry went from 60%-70% to 70%-80%, and the fee-related share from 20%-25% to 15%-20% [S30] REPORTED; the new ranges match KKR's own deck [S5] CONFIRMED.

Say this in the interview

"Because KKR pays from one pool and most pay comes from carry, a person in client solutions and a person on a deal team want the same thing: funds that make money for clients. That is what an LP wants to hear when they ask about alignment, and I think it is a real selling point for the KCS team." [S2, S5] INFERRED

KKR's balance sheet and its shareholders

KKR's own money is invested next to clients'. At 31 December 2025, KKR and its employees had about $30bn invested in or committed to KKR funds and companies [S12] CONFIRMED. KKR says these "GP commitments" are usually required by contract, and also show "conviction"; it adds that their size has fallen relative to fund sizes as funds grew [S2] CONFIRMED. Employees and others put $612m of their own cash into KKR vehicles in 2025, mostly without paying fees or carry [S2] CONFIRMED.

Shareholders own KKR & Co. Inc. They get a dividend that KKR says it has raised every year since becoming a corporation in 2018: $0.78 a year from Q1 2026 [S1, S4] CONFIRMED. Until the Sunset Date (see section G) they cannot elect directors [S2] CONFIRMED. 891.6m shares were outstanding on 24 Feb 2026 [S2] CONFIRMED.

D. The operating model: four layers and what flows between them@@f-model@@

The simplest way to picture KKR is as four stacked layers. Clients sit on top. The investments sit at the bottom. In between are the teams that bring money in and the teams that put it to work. The KCS team, the one you are applying to, sits in the second layer and touches every other layer.

Three flows matter most for a KCS candidate. First, KCS is a two-way channel. It takes products to clients and brings client demand back to the investment teams. The Frankfurt KCS intern advert says the team "seeks to 'connect the dots' across all businesses at KKR, from our Private Equity investing teams to Infrastructure, Real Estate, Credit, Capital Markets and Insurance-Funded Strategies" [S390] CONFIRMED. Second, KCS and KCM work together on co-investment and syndication, which is where much of KKR's remaining deal-fee income now comes from, because fund-related deal fees are credited to LPs [S2] CONFIRMED; the link is the author's INFERRED. Third, Global Atlantic is both an engine and a client: its assets are managed by KKR's credit teams, and KKR reports "Total Insurance Economics" of $2.0bn over the 12 months to Q2 2026, which adds those fees to the insurance earnings [S1] CONFIRMED.

Governance and risk: who says yes, who keeps watch@@f-governance@@

KKR runs risk through committees, not single decision-makers. The 10-K says: "Our investment committees, or similar committees, review and evaluate investment opportunities using frameworks that are designed to include qualitative and quantitative assessments of the key investment risks" [S2] CONFIRMED. Committees exist per strategy and region. In London, for example, Tara Davies sits on the Infrastructure Investment Committee and the Infrastructure Portfolio Management Committee, and Mattia Caprioli on the European Private Equity Investment Committee and European Portfolio Management Committee [S16, S17] CONFIRMED.

Why this matters

LPs ask about governance in their due diligence questionnaires. A KCS junior helps answer them. Knowing that decisions go through named committees, and that pay is set on the whole firm's results, lets you explain why one bad deal does not lead a team to take wild risks to catch up. Lewin's line from 30 July 2026 sums it up: "Relationships travel, ideas travel, lessons learned travel" [S3] CONFIRMED.

E. How the business mix has changed@@f-mix@@

The single most useful sentence about KKR's evolution is in its own 10-K: "As of December 31, 2010, our traditional Private Equity strategy represented over 70% of our total AUM. As of December 31, 2025, traditional Private Equity was less than 25% of our total AUM" [S2] CONFIRMED. Fees tell the same story. Real Assets management fees almost tripled between 2021 and 2025 and now nearly match private equity [S2] CONFIRMED.

On 30 July 2026 CFO Rob Lewin listed growth since the April 2024 Investor Day: private equity up about 45%, infrastructure doubled, credit up about 35%, Asia up over 35%, third-party insurance up over 50%, and wealth up about six times [S3] CONFIRMED. Wealth is the outlier: K-Series grew from $16bn at the end of 2024 to $42bn in June 2026 [S1, S5] CONFIRMED.

Your opinion goes here

A defensible view: "KKR is becoming less of a buyout firm and more of a capital solutions platform. Credit is its biggest line, insurance is a whole segment, and wealth grew about six times in two years. That makes the client solutions job more complex, because you are now matching dozens of products to very different clients." Then add your own angle: which of these shifts do you find most interesting, and why? [S2, S3] INFERRED

F. A public company: why that is a gift for your research@@f-public@@

KKR has traded on the New York Stock Exchange since July 2010 (ticker KKR), after first listing in Amsterdam in October 2009 [S5] CONFIRMED [S28] REPORTED. It became a corporation on 1 July 2018 and joined the S&P 500 on 24 June 2024 [S2, S31] CONFIRMED. Being listed means KKR must publish a lot about itself. Most private firms you could apply to publish almost nothing. Use this.

What you can read for free on ir.kkr.com or SEC EDGAR: the 10-K annual report (FY2025 filed 27 Feb 2026), with fee ranges, fund terms, risks, legal cases and the founding fund track records [S1, S2]; the quarterly 10-Q [S332]; the quarterly earnings release, with a fund-by-fund table of sizes, dates and returns (Q3 2026 due 9 Nov 2026) [S1, S333]; the earnings call, the source of most management quotes in this pack [S3]; 8-Ks for material events such as Arctos, shareholder votes and the DOJ settlement [S6, S7, S8, S349]; and proxy and Investor Day decks (last full Investor Day 10 Apr 2024) [S5, S9] CONFIRMED.

How to read KKR's earnings release in 10 minutes

Say this in the interview

"I read the Q2 2026 release. What stood out was that KKR raised $305bn since the start of 2024, beating its three-year $300bn target in two and a half years, and that management said it was the strongest monetisation quarter in its history. For a client team, both halves matter: new money in, and cash back to LPs, which is what earns the next commitment." [S1, S3, S330]

G. Leadership and the future@@f-leaders@@

Who runs KKR

RolePersonBackground (public, professional)
Co-Chief Executive OfficersJoseph (Joe) Bae and Scott NuttallBoth joined KKR in 1996; Co-Presidents and Co-COOs from July 2017; co-CEOs from 11 Oct 2021. Bae built KKR Asia and had led or served on all private markets investment committees. Nuttall built the listing, balance sheet, credit, capital markets, capital raising and insurance businesses [S10] CONFIRMED.
Co-Executive ChairmenHenry Kravis and George RobertsCo-founders; co-CEOs 1987 to 2021 [S2, S10] CONFIRMED.
Chief Financial OfficerRobert (Rob) LewinLeads the earnings calls with the co-CEOs [S2, S3] CONFIRMED.
Chief Administrative Officer; Chief Legal OfficerDane Holmes; Kathryn SudolHolmes is ex Goldman Sachs [S2] CONFIRMED.
Head of Global Client SolutionsEric Mogelof, Partner, New YorkJoined 2020 from PIMCO (17 years there); also oversees Global Marketing [S18] CONFIRMED. (The KCS section covers the team in depth.)

When the founders handed over, Bae and Nuttall said: "We have spent virtually our entire careers at KKR because Henry and George are visionaries who not only shaped the business world but created a really special firm" [S10] CONFIRMED. Note the pattern: KKR grows its leaders from inside and over decades.

Investor Day 2024: targets and progress

On 10 April 2024 KKR set public targets for 2026 and beyond [S9] CONFIRMED. By mid 2026 the fundraising and fee targets were met, while the targets that depend on selling assets were behind. On 30 July 2026 Lewin said of the $7 ANI target: "as it relates to $7, we had removed obviously, that formal guidance last quarter. I'd say, in many ways, it has provided a bit of a distraction" [S3] CONFIRMED. Earlier in 2026 management had stressed it needed a "conducive market environment" for exits and had "modestly less visibility" [S39, S40] REPORTED.

Your opinion goes here

A balanced line: "The $7 miss looks more like a timing story than a business story. The targets KKR controls, raising money and growing fees, were hit early. The miss is in realisations, which depend on markets. I would also note two real headwinds: more competition in insurance, where Lewin said KKR will allocate 'a little bit less capital', and the Asian Fund II clawback." [S1, S3, S4] INFERRED

The Sunset Date, explained simply

In October 2021, alongside the CEO succession, KKR signed a Reorganization Agreement [S2, S10] CONFIRMED. Its last step is the Sunset Date. In the 10-K's words: "On the 'Sunset Date' (which will occur no later than December 31, 2026), KKR will cancel the Series I preferred stock, establish voting rights for all common stock on a one vote per share basis, and acquire control of the carry pool" [S2] CONFIRMED. Today, ordinary shareholders cannot elect or remove directors: the holder of the Series I preferred share, KKR Management LLP (owned by senior employees including Kravis and Roberts), appoints them. KKR uses the NYSE "controlled company" exemptions [S2] CONFIRMED. On 29 May 2026 directors were again elected by KKR Management LLP [S352] CONFIRMED.

In April 2026 shareholders approved three charter changes to prepare: meetings only (no written consent), the board fills vacancies, and the board fixes its own size [S6] CONFIRMED. The fourth, removing the 90% supermajority, failed for lack of quorum at the reconvened meeting on 21 May 2026, even though 97.83% of votes cast were in favour [S7] CONFIRMED.

Say this in the interview

"By the end of 2026 KKR becomes a normal one-share-one-vote company. The founders' special control ends 50 years after they started the firm. I see it as the last step of a handover that began with the co-CEOs in 2021, and something an institutional client who is also a shareholder might well ask about." [S2, S10] INFERRED

What leadership says about the future

  • Four growth drivers (Lewin, 30 Jul 2026): a growing industry with megatrends (AI, digital and energy infrastructure, defence); Asia (about 60% of expected global GDP growth); retirement demand from ageing populations; and a model that grows earnings without big headcount growth [S3] CONFIRMED.
  • Market mood (Nuttall): "In our time here, I don't recall a period of time where the external perception is so disconnected from the operating fundamentals and how it feels inside the firm." And: "Our industry is increasingly K-shaped... We find ourselves on the happy part of the K" [S3] CONFIRMED.
  • Five worries answered (Nuttall): private credit anxiety (KKR expects a record third-party credit fundraising year); wealth redemptions (K-Series net inflows up 20%+ year to date); PE exits (record monetisation quarter); software and AI (about 6% of AUM); slowing fundraising (KKR expects a record year) [S3] CONFIRMED [S362] REPORTED.
  • Big goals: "Multiple paths to surpass $1 trillion of AUM in the next 5 years" and "Strong conviction we can double Global Atlantic AUM" [S5, S9] CONFIRMED (targets).
Author's inference from hiring and moves

Recent senior hires and launches point to five priorities INFERRED: (1) distribution and wealth: Capital Group partnership, Doha Bank MOU signed by David Petraeus, KKR Middle East chairman (21 Sep 2026), new Asia-Pacific client head Bhavit Patel (Jun 2026) and a KCS Principal hire in Hong Kong [S22, S358, S359, S367]; (2) AI and power infrastructure: Helix, led by former AWS CEO Adam Selipsky [S3]; (3) secondaries and "solutions": Arctos and KKR Solutions under Ian Charles [S38, S355]; (4) insurance and Asia know-how: former Manulife CEO Roy Gori as senior adviser [S3]; (5) European policy and plumbing: Philippe De Backer for European public affairs (London) and Andre Serpa as EMEA Head of Treasury [S41, S42]. Each of these creates new products for KCS to explain. Treat the pattern as your reading, not KKR's stated plan.

I. The skeletons, told straight@@f-skeletons@@

Every 50-year-old investment firm has deals that went wrong and fines it paid. Interviewers rarely raise them, but a client asks about them in due diligence, and knowing them calmly is a sign of maturity. Here they are, with the facts and KKR's response.

IssueWhat happenedKKR's response and status
RJR Nabisco (1988 to 1989)KKR won a bidding war at $109 a share against management's $112, because the board judged KKR's bid more certain. About $25bn of equity value, about $31bn with debt; the subject of "Barbarians at the Gate" [S27, S28] REPORTED. One history says Kravis "clearly overpaid". KKR's own 10-K shows the 1987 Fund behind it made 8.9% net IRR and 2.4x, against 34.4% gross IRR for the 1986 Fund [S2, S27] CONFIRMED.No new LBOs for about three years after 1989; remaining stake traded for Borden in 1995 [S27] REPORTED. Fame, weak returns.
TXU / Energy Future Holdings (2007 to 2014)With TPG and Goldman Sachs' PE arm, bought TXU for about $45bn, the largest LBO ever. A bet that gas prices would rise; they fell. Chapter 11 on 29 Apr 2014 with about $49.7bn of debt; equity largely wiped out [S28, S32] CONFIRMED.A lesson in leverage plus a commodity bet. Shows why KKR now stresses durable cash flows INFERRED.
Toys "R" Us (2005 to 2018)With Bain Capital and Vornado, bought for about $6.6bn. Bankrupt September 2017, liquidated 2018 [S28, S33] REPORTED.KKR and Bain each put $10m into a $20m fund for laid-off workers (Nov 2018), not legally required; advocates said about $75m was needed [S33] REPORTED.
SEC broken-deal expenses (29 Jun 2015)The SEC found KKR misallocated more than $17m of costs from deals that never happened to its flagship PE funds instead of sharing them with co-investors, including KKR executives. "The first SEC case to charge a private equity adviser with misallocating broken deal expenses" [S20] CONFIRMED.Paid nearly $30m (over $14m disgorgement, over $4.5m interest, $10m penalty) without admitting or denying. KKR said it related to "historical ... policies and not to any current practices" [S20] CONFIRMED [S45] REPORTED.
Kentucky pension suits (2017 to now)Claims over accounts run by Prisma Capital Partners, a former KKR subsidiary, for Kentucky Retirement Systems; Kravis and Roberts named personally. The 2017 case was dismissed for lack of standing (final Feb 2024). The Attorney General's 2020 action and member suits continue; the Kentucky Supreme Court took up jurisdiction and indemnity issues (briefs Sep 2025) [S2] CONFIRMED.Contesting. Outcome not known in our sources as of Oct 2026.
SEC off-channel messages (Jan 2025)One of 12 firms fined $63.1m in total for staff using unapproved messaging apps for business. KKR paid $11m [S29] REPORTED.Settled. An industry-wide sweep, not a KKR-only case.
Asian Fund II clawback (Q4 2025)The 2013 fund ($5.8bn) had paid carry it later had to give back. $344m repaid; $207m net after recovery from current and former staff. 2025 ANI was $4.87 a share, or $5.05 without it [S1, S2, S4] CONFIRMED.Paid. The LP contract worked as designed.
DOJ Hart-Scott-Rodino (2025 to 2026)The DOJ alleged KKR broke US pre-merger filing rules on at least 16 deals in 2021 and 2022: altered documents for 8, omitted documents for 10, no filing for 2. 26 Aug 2026: proposed $250m civil penalty, the largest ever for HSR [S2, S21] CONFIRMED.KKR first sued, calling the penalties unconstitutional; then settled. It said it "acted in good faith", that "We strongly disagree with the Antitrust Division's characterization", and that the penalty "will have no financial impact on the firm, our funds, or any of our investors and will be fully reimbursed by outside law firms". Court approval pending [S21, S349] CONFIRMED.

The pattern in KKR's responses INFERRED: settle without admitting fault (SEC 2015, SEC 2025, DOJ 2026); stress that the issue is historical and practices have changed; fight first where it sees a principle (the DOJ countersuit); and occasionally make voluntary gestures (the Toys "R" Us fund).

How to talk about this if asked

1. Acknowledge, briefly and with facts. "Yes, RJR is the deal that made KKR famous, but KKR's own filings show the fund behind it returned 8.9% a year, well below its other early funds."

2. Separate type from size. "The recent issues are process ones: a filing case settled for $250m that KKR says outside law firms will reimburse, and an industry-wide messaging fine. They are not about investor losses."

3. Show what changed. "Since 2014 KKR's funds credit 100% of fund-related deal fees to LPs, and in 2025 it repaid a clawback on Asian Fund II. That is the contract protecting clients."

4. Link to the job. "In client solutions you would point LPs to the approved public statement, never improvise, and make sure due diligence answers match the filings." [S2, S4, S349] INFERRED

Don't say this

"KKR was fined for fraud" (no: the DOJ case is about pre-merger filings, and KKR disputed it). "RJR was a great deal" (KKR's own numbers say otherwise). "Barbarians" as a joke about the firm. And do not volunteer the skeletons unprompted; answer calmly if asked [S2, S21] INFERRED.

What these numbers do and do not mean

They do mean: the London LLP is a substantial team (about 182 employees plus 88 members, so roughly 270 people in this one entity INFERRED), its costs are rising, and it is run as a sub-adviser to the US parent "in connection with a number of Private Markets funds" [S25] CONFIRMED.

They do not mean: that KKR's London business "earns £177m". Say this in the interview

@@k3@@
Part 3

What KCS is: KKR's client engine

The team you want to join: where it came from, how big it is, who runs it, who its clients are, what it sells, how it is organised and how it is wired into the rest of KKR.

KCS in one paragraph@@k3-one@@

KKR Global Client Solutions (KCS) is the team that brings money into KKR and looks after the people who gave it. KKR's own job advert calls it "KKR's dedicated investor solutions team" and says it "was first formed in 2009 to invest in and focus on KKR's relationships with current and potential investors" [S103] CONFIRMED. A February 2026 posting puts the team at "~320 employees" [S106] REPORTED; an October 2026 posting says "over 300 executives located in over 20 [offices] across four continents" [S141] CONFIRMED. It is organised around "two specialized focus areas: Sales/Relationship Management and Product/Strategy Management" [S141] CONFIRMED, and its stated job is to "connect the dots" across every KKR business, "from our Private Equity investing teams to Infrastructure, Real Estate, Credit, Capital Markets and Insurance-Funded Strategies" [S141] CONFIRMED.

Put plainly: KKR runs pooled funds. Before any fund can buy a company, a wind farm or a loan, outside investors must promise money to it. Those investors are called limited partners or, in KKR's newer language, clients. KCS finds them, explains the products, answers their questions, gets them signed up, reports to them for ten years or more, and then asks them to back the next fund [S103, S101] CONFIRMED. That is why the same posting that lists "fundraising activities" also lists "reporting requirements" and "ongoing servicing of existing clients" [S101] CONFIRMED. Selling and servicing are one job.

Key term

Limited partner (LP) / client: an investor that commits money to a KKR fund, such as a pension fund, a sovereign wealth fund, an insurer, a family office or (now) a wealthy individual through a private bank. "Limited" because their liability is limited to what they put in. General partner (GP): the manager that runs the fund, here KKR.

Why this matters

Fundraising is the fuel for KKR's fees. New capital raised was $34bn in Q2 2026 and a record $133bn over the twelve months to 30 June 2026 [S74] CONFIRMED. KKR says it raised $305bn from the start of 2024, beating its $300bn three-year target in about two and a half years [S76] REPORTED. That number is, in effect, KCS's scoreboard INFERRED.

History: from the Client and Partner Group to KCS@@k3-history@@

KKR was founded in 1976 [S70] CONFIRMED. The modern client team is much younger than the firm. In 2009 KKR hired Suzanne Donohoe "to lead KKR's Client and Partner Group, a global team responsible for supporting and interacting with KKR's Limited Partners" [S94] REPORTED. KKR's own adverts date KCS to the same year [S103] CONFIRMED.

The 2009 to 2020 period built the institutional machine. KKR says the group raised "over $225 billion from a global client base", grew from supporting 4 investment strategies in 2008 to 24 in 2020, and "more than quadrupled the number of clients KKR serves" [S94] REPORTED. In 2010 Jim Burns arrived from Morgan Stanley and "established, and led for eleven years, KKR's Individual Investor Business", covering "family offices and wealth platforms globally" [S122] CONFIRMED. The Family Capital business was set up in 2014 [S178] CONFIRMED, the same year KKR bought Avoca, the origin of its Dublin credit team [S152] CONFIRMED.

The 2020 onward period is the wealth pivot. In August 2020 Donohoe became KKR's first Global Head of Strategic Growth and Eric Mogelof, who spent 17 years at PIMCO including running its US global wealth management business, took over the client group [S94, S79] CONFIRMED. In January 2022 KKR created a Global Head of Private Wealth role inside the group [S97] REPORTED. The evergreen "K-Series" funds for individuals followed in 2022 and 2023 [S111, S112, S113] CONFIRMED, then the Capital Group partnership in 2024 [S86] CONFIRMED. Some time after early 2022 the name changed to Global Client Solutions; the exact date was not found [S138] INFERRED.

Say this in the interview

"KCS is younger than most of KKR. It was set up in 2009, and in its first eleven years it went from supporting 4 strategies to 24. Since 2020, under Eric Mogelof, who ran wealth at PIMCO, the big build has been private wealth and partnerships like Capital Group. So the team I would join is in its second act." [S94, S79, S86]

The mission in KKR's own words@@k3-mission@@

KKR describes the team's purpose in a handful of recurring phrases. Learn them; they are the vocabulary the interviewers use.

KKR's words (verbatim)WhereWhat it tells you
"KKR's dedicated investor solutions team ... first formed in 2009 to invest in and focus on KKR's relationships with current and potential investors"GWS Internal Sales posting, Aug 2026 [S103]Relationships are the product. "Current and potential" means both service and new business.
"seeks to 'connect the dots' across all businesses at KKR"Frankfurt KCS intern posting, Oct 2026 [S141]KCS is the joining layer between investing teams and clients.
"to diversify KKR's client base to include new investors, across all regions and institution types, and to raise capital for the Firm's expanding product platform"Frankfurt posting [S141]Two goals: more kinds of client, more products sold.
"including a growing focus on individual, private wealth investors"Singapore KCS intern posting, Aug 2026 [S107]Wealth is the growth frontier.
"work with institutional and wealth management investors across the world to understand their investment needs, deliver world-class alternatives solutions, and provide customized client service"Eric Mogelof bio [S79]Needs first, then solutions, then service.
"We subscribe to the view of Henry Kravis and George Roberts that people do business with those they like and trust."Jim Burns, kkr.com [S81]The founders' culture line, applied to clients.
"with one P&L where most places have silos ... 'One Firm,' collaboration, operating with 'like and trust' are core to how KKR operates."Singapore posting [S107]Why KCS can sell any strategy without internal turf wars.

The "one P&L" line is backed by the 10-K: KKR's asset management operating expenses "are shared across a single expense pool given the collaborative nature of our five business lines" [S70] CONFIRMED. That matters for KCS. A relationship manager covering a Dutch pension fund does not need to negotiate with the infrastructure team about who "owns" the client or who gets credit; the firm is paid as one INFERRED.

Your opinion goes here

Pick one phrase and say why it rings true for you. Suggested angle: "connect the dots" describes the job better than "sales", because the London analyst posting lists eight internal teams the analyst must work with to answer one client [S101]. Then add your own experience of being the person who joins things up.

How big is KCS?@@k3-size@@

KKR does not publish a KCS headcount in its filings. Three kinds of public evidence exist, and they agree reasonably well.

~320
KCS employees, Dublin posting, Feb 2026 [S106] REPORTED. Oct 2026 posting: "over 300 executives" [S141]
232
KCS bios at Principal level and above in KKR's public directory, 11 Oct 2026 [S80, S149] CONFIRMED
20
of those 232 based in London (19 if a dual-listed San Francisco/London bio is excluded) [S149, S80]

The directory breaks the 232 into 84 Principals, 80 Directors, 51 Managing Directors and 17 Partners and titled heads [S80] CONFIRMED. It does not list Analysts or Associates. An older summer-analyst posting described "roughly 270 professionals", date unclear [S108] REPORTED. For scale, KKR had 5,043 employees at 31 December 2025, of whom 2,705 worked in asset management [S70] CONFIRMED; ~320 is about 12% of that asset management headcount INFERRED.

Estimate: method and as-of date (11 Oct 2026)

Step 1, count. KKR's directory lists 232 KCS people at Principal and above worldwide, 46 in EMEA and 20 in London [S149] CONFIRMED.

Step 2, anchor the total. Two KKR postings say ~320 (Feb 2026) and "over 300" (Oct 2026) [S106, S141]. So the directory covers roughly 70 to 75% of the team; the gap of about 70 to 90 is mostly Analysts and Associates INFERRED.

Step 3, scale EMEA. EMEA is 46 of 232 senior bios, about 20%. 20% of ~320 is about 64. Allowing for a higher junior ratio in Europe (London and Frankfurt are hiring juniors now [S140, S141]) gives an estimate of 55 to 90 KCS people in EMEA, central ~65, and 25 to 35 in London (medium-low confidence) INFERRED.

Caveats. Some Dublin client-service (CAPS) staff may or may not be counted inside KCS. Bios can lag moves.

Who leads it@@k3-leaders@@

All of the following is public professional information from KKR's own website. Titles change; check kkr.com before naming anyone in an interview, and name people only when it is relevant.

Person and titleBasePublic background and what the role tells you

Jim Burns, Partner, Head of Institutional Client Solutions, AmericasNew YorkBuilt the individual investor business from 2010; led EMEA clients from London 2018 to 2023; sat on the Executive Committee of KKR Capital Markets LLC [S122] CONFIRMED.

Doug Krupa, Partner, Head of Global Wealth Solutions, AmericasNew York"Led the development of KKR's evergreen solutions"; 8 years at Blackstone in private wealth product strategy [S123] CONFIRMED. Made Partner from 1 Jan 2026 [S165].
