Source uncertain

No one on kkr.com is titled "Head of KCS EMEA" (October 2026). Mark Danzey's "European Head of Institutional Client Solutions" is the closest [S156]; Markus Egloff leads wealth internationally [S157]; Doug Brody leads EMEA family capital from New York [S125]. Reporting lines are not published, so any org chart, including the one in this part, is a reconstruction INFERRED. Names that circulate informally, such as "Alisa Amarosa Wood" as a KCS leader, are not in the current KCS directory [S80]; she appears in 2025 as a co-leader of evergreen private equity strategies [S177]. Do not guess titles in the interview.

The three client channels@@k3-channels@@

KKR presents its clients in three segments on kkr.com: Institutional Investors, Family Capital and Global Wealth [S195] CONFIRMED. Insurance has become a fourth client relationship with its own team and its own products [S104, S127] CONFIRMED. For a beginner it is easiest to think in three channels, with family capital sitting between institutions and wealth.

Channel A: Institutional

Corporate and public pensions, sovereign wealth funds, insurers, endowments, foundations, health care organisations, and the investment consultants who advise them [S81] CONFIRMED. They mostly buy closed-end "drawdown" funds plus separately managed accounts and co-investments [S70] CONFIRMED. The 10-K warns that sovereign funds and public pensions increasingly prefer "alternatives to traditional fund structures, such as separately managed accounts ... and, in some cases, consolidating their capital with fewer alternative asset managers" [S70] CONFIRMED. That consolidation favours large multi-strategy firms like KKR INFERRED. CalPERS, for example, has backed KKR's North America, Europe and Asia flagships over 16 years, including $600m to North America Fund XIII [S117] CONFIRMED.

Channel B: Private wealth and family capital

KKR's 10-K: "Over the last five years, we have focused on private wealth as a key addressable market ... Our private wealth capital comes from multiple sources, including wirehouses, independent broker-dealers, registered investment advisers, global private banks, and family offices" [S70] CONFIRMED. A wirehouse is a big US broker with thousands of advisers; an RIA is an independent adviser firm; a private bank serves wealthy clients, and is the key route in Europe and Asia INFERRED. Family Capital is a separate team for single-family offices and founders, offering "Co-Investment Opportunities", "Bespoke Separately Managed Accounts", "Two-Way Sourcing Dialogues" and "Comprehensive Debt Solutions" [S84] CONFIRMED.

Channel C: Insurance and strategic partners

Global Atlantic, KKR's insurer, is fully owned since January 2024 [S70] CONFIRMED. It "sponsors co-invest vehicles that raise third-party capital to participate alongside Global Atlantic through reinsurance" (often called sidecars) [S70] CONFIRMED; management cited $62bn of AUM in these vehicles in mid-2026 [S77] REPORTED. A dedicated KCS team raises that money [S128] CONFIRMED, while the Global Insurance Client Solutions team builds "multi-dimensional, senior-level relationships with insurance companies globally" [S104] CONFIRMED. Strategic partners include sovereign investors who co-found platforms (Kuwait Investment Authority in Helix Digital Infrastructure) [S78] REPORTED and manager partners such as Capital Group [S86] CONFIRMED.

KKR's investor mix: who the money comes from@@k3-mix@@

KKR's FY2025 10-K includes a pie chart of AUM by investor type [S71] CONFIRMED. It is the single best picture of who KCS serves. Two facts stand out. First, private wealth (18%) is now bigger than pensions and other institutions (14%). Second, insurance in total (Global Atlantic's own balance sheet at 22% plus third-party insurers at 11%) is about a third of AUM [S71] INFERRED.

Geography: KKR's investors span 65 countries [S70] CONFIRMED. On the Q2 2026 call Scott Nuttall said "roughly 40%" of recent activity comes from outside the US [S77] REPORTED. KKR does not publish a count of clients, a re-up rate or how many clients invest in more than one strategy [S70, S74] (gap). If an interviewer asks, say you looked and it is not disclosed.

Don't say this

"Most of KKR's money comes from pension funds." It did once. Today pensions and other institutions are 14% of AUM, behind Global Atlantic (22%) and private wealth (18%) [S71]. Also avoid "KKR is the biggest in private wealth": Blackstone's private wealth business is far larger (about $324bn against KKR's $42bn K-Series) [S216, S73] REPORTED.

What KCS sells: the product shelf@@k3-shelf@@

A KCS professional does not sell one fund. KKR supported 24 strategies by 2020 [S94] and Nuttall said in 2024 that of $214bn raised from 2022 to mid-2024, "only $14 billion ... was in flagships" [S119] REPORTED. The shelf has four layers.

Shelf 1: flagship and strategy drawdown funds

A drawdown fund takes promises (commitments) from investors, then "calls" the cash over the investment period, which for infrastructure and real estate can run up to six years, with fund terms of 10 to 13 years [S2] CONFIRMED. Recent examples: North America Fund XIV closed at about $23bn in April 2026 [S335] CONFIRMED; Global Infrastructure Investors V closed at $19.2bn on 3 August 2026, KKR's largest infrastructure fund, with investors including "pension plans, sovereign wealth funds, insurance companies, asset managers, private wealth platforms, and family offices" [S176] CONFIRMED. That investor list is literally the KCS client map INFERRED.

Shelf 2: the K-Series evergreen funds

K-Series funds have no end date. Investors subscribe regularly and can ask to redeem a limited amount periodically [S70] CONFIRMED. Nuttall: "K Series is built to be able to go to the accredited investor in the U.S., which is $1 million and up in net worth" [S76] REPORTED. The main US classes of K-PEC and K-INFRA charge a 1.25% annual management fee [S111, S112] CONFIRMED. About 85% of K-Series assets are in private equity and infrastructure [S76] REPORTED. London is home to the EMEA product lead for K-PRIME and K-PEC, Matt Yates [S133] CONFIRMED.

The growth has not been frictionless. In Q1 2026, K-FIT investors asked to redeem 6.3% of shares and the fund paid about 80% of requests pro rata; in Q2 requests fell to 1.65% and were paid in full [S338] REPORTED. Nuttall's answer on the call: "What you don't read about in the articles is the inflows. But we're up 20% net year-to-date" [S77] REPORTED. Explaining liquidity terms honestly, before and after the sale, is now core KCS work INFERRED.

Shelf 3: partner products

The Capital Group partnership, announced in May 2024 as "an exclusive strategic partnership designed to help broaden access to private market investment opportunities" [S86] CONFIRMED, launched two public-private credit interval funds on 29 April 2025: about 60% public fixed income and 40% private credit, with quarterly repurchase offers of up to 10% of shares [S92] CONFIRMED. Capital Group "maintains relationships with more than 200,000 financial advisors across the United States" [S92] CONFIRMED. Capital Group KKR U.S. Equity+ followed, and its private side "invests in a K-Series private equity vehicle" [S70] CONFIRMED. In the UK, Quilter Cheviot began offering KKR's evergreen private equity strategy, a launch Markus Egloff called "an important milestone in our efforts to deliver greater access to KKR's strategies" [S177] CONFIRMED.

Shelf 4: customised solutions

This is what the team description means by "able to deliver customized products". It includes separately managed accounts (a fund with one investor and its own terms), co-investments (a stake in one specific deal alongside a KKR fund, usually at low or no fee), strategic partnerships (multi-year, multi-asset mandates), multi-asset portfolios, and insurance "fully integrated balance sheet solutions" [S84, S85, S104] CONFIRMED. KKR's macro team frames the client conversation with the Total Portfolio Approach, "a governance and investment framework that seeks to improve capital allocation by allowing investors to evaluate opportunities across the total portfolio rather than through static asset class silos" [S90] CONFIRMED.

Key terms

Interval fund: a US registered fund that offers to buy back a set slice of shares at regular intervals. BDC: business development company, a US vehicle for lending to private companies; K-FIT elected BDC status in 2023 [S113]. Feeder fund: a vehicle that pools many small investors into one ticket into a KKR fund [S114]. Accredited investor: in the US, broadly an individual with $1m+ net worth [S76].

How KCS is organised@@k3-org@@

KKR's Frankfurt posting gives the official skeleton: two focus areas, "Sales/Relationship Management and Product/Strategy Management" [S141] CONFIRMED. The brief's team description adds the third layer: "Junior resources serving in a generalist capacity". Around them sit enabling teams that the job adverts name: the CAPS team for tenders and due diligence questionnaires [S106] CONFIRMED, client operations [S138], marketing [S79, S138] and wealth communications [S147] CONFIRMED.

How the three layers divide the work:

  • Relationship managers (RMs) own a territory or client list. They set meetings, run roadshows, pitch, and close commitments. Josh Metz, for example, "leads a team of Relationship Managers across the U.S." in wealth [S126] CONFIRMED. In Europe, RMs are split by country: UK, DACH, France/Benelux/Southern Europe, Nordics, Middle East [S150, S153, S154, S155, S151] CONFIRMED.
  • Product specialists are the experts on one asset class. A Dublin posting says the credit team "leads fundraising activities and will also be responsible for owning marketing materials, developing thought leadership and leading investor diligence processes", and is "a group of over 30 product strategists" [S106] CONFIRMED.
  • Junior generalists support several RMs and products at once. In London that means reporting, fundraising support, KYC onboarding, answering client requests and events [S101] CONFIRMED. Part 4 decodes this line by line.
  • CAPS (Client and Product Services) answers tenders and due diligence questionnaires from Dublin and New York [S106, S146] CONFIRMED.
Why this matters

The split explains who you would sit next to. As an intern in London you would most likely support RMs covering EMEA institutions and family offices, or a product team such as infrastructure, which is the biggest product cluster in London [S150] CONFIRMED. You will learn both the client and the product, which is the point of a generalist seat INFERRED.

Why a central client team exists@@k3-hub@@

Imagine KKR without KCS. Each investing team (private equity, infrastructure, real estate, credit, insurance, capital markets) would run its own investor relations. A large pension fund would get six sets of calls, six sets of due diligence questionnaires, six versions of KKR's story, and nobody who sees the whole relationship. With 24 strategies supported by 2020 [S94] and investors in 65 countries [S70], the number of separate links would explode INFERRED.

A central team, the "wheel" in the figure below, does four things the "tangle" cannot INFERRED:

  1. One view of each client. The RM knows everything the client owns with KKR and what it needs next. That is what makes cross-selling possible, and KKR's own adverts call it a "Relationship-focused, solutions-oriented approach".
  2. Reuse. One library of due diligence answers (the CAPS team) instead of six [S106].
  3. Consistency and compliance. One approved story, one set of numbers. That matters because marketing to investors in the UK and EU is regulated [S70] CONFIRMED.
  4. Leverage for big clients. Large investors are "consolidating their capital with fewer alternative asset managers" [S70] CONFIRMED. A single team that can offer every strategy is how KKR wins that consolidation.
Say this in the interview

"Without KCS, a big pension fund would deal with every KKR strategy separately. With it, the client has one relationship, one set of answers and one person who knows its whole portfolio. That is why the team description talks about an 'integrated approach' and why the one-P&L culture matters: nobody fights over who owns the client." [S70, S107]

How KCS is wired into the rest of KKR@@k3-wiring@@

KCS has three kinds of connection inside the firm. Embedded links sit inside the investing businesses. Connective links join KCS to KKR's other client-facing engines: Capital Markets, Global Atlantic and Capstone. Utility links are the control and service functions every client answer depends on.

Embedded: the investing teams

Product specialists are the bridge. Credit strategists "work closely with ... Portfolio managers and deal teams to understand the current portfolio, deal pipeline and overall market dynamics" [S106] CONFIRMED. The head of infrastructure product strategy is also the Chief Development Officer of KKR Infrastructure, and was the KKR voice in the GII V close: "We are grateful to receive strong support from both longstanding clients who have partnered with us across multiple fund vintages and new investors from around the world" [S138, S334] CONFIRMED. The traffic runs both ways. Investing teams give KCS track record, deal stories and senior people for client meetings; KCS brings back what clients want, which shapes new products [S141] CONFIRMED (the framing is INFERRED).

Connective: KCM, Global Atlantic, Capstone

KKR Capital Markets "provides syndication services for co-investments in transactions participated in by KKR, our investment vehicles, Global Atlantic, and third-party clients" [S70] CONFIRMED. KCM earned $930m of transaction fees in 2025 [S70] CONFIRMED. KCS knows which clients want which deals; KCM structures and places them INFERRED. The people links are dense: Jim Burns sat on KCM's Executive Committee while leading EMEA clients [S122]; Lauren Hahn moved from KCM equity capital markets to head PE product strategy [S129]; Doug Brody ran the KCM co-investments team before heading Family Capital [S125]; and in Europe Mark Danzey heads both KCM and institutional client solutions [S156] CONFIRMED.

Global Atlantic is both a source of capital and a client channel. The Global Insurance Client Solutions principal works with "reinsurance pricing/deal teams" and the "Insurance-Funded Product Strategies team to structure and execute third-party capital vehicles" [S104] CONFIRMED. KKR Capstone, the in-house operating team, does not raise a fund; its value-creation work is part of the story KCS tells investors about how returns are made [S174] INFERRED.

Utility: legal, compliance, risk, operations, finance

The London analyst posting is explicit: the junior answers client requests by working with "Product teams, Investment teams, Operations, Finance, Legal, Compliance, Risk" [S101] CONFIRMED. KYC onboarding is a named task [S101]. The person who leads KKR's product strategy sits on the Global Conflicts and Compliance Committee [S121] CONFIRMED, a sign that product design and compliance are joined at the top INFERRED.

Your opinion goes here

Which link is most underrated? A defensible view: the KCM link. Co-investment is what large clients increasingly want, KKR can underwrite more of a deal than its fund needs, and KCS is the team that knows who will take the rest [S70]. Danzey's dual role in Europe suggests KKR thinks the same [S156]. Add one sentence on why that interests you personally.

KCS in London and EMEA: the team map@@k3-emea@@

KKR's directory lists 46 KCS people at Principal level and above in EMEA: London 20, Dubai and Riyadh 6, Dublin 5, Zurich 5, Paris 4, Stockholm 4, Frankfurt 2 [S149] CONFIRMED. Their titles split into about 14 Managing Directors, 15 Directors and 17 Principals [S149] CONFIRMED. KKR's London office as a whole is estimated at about 300 to 400 people, based on Companies House accounts (182 average employees plus 88 members in the main LLP in 2025) and 155 London senior bios [S171, S149] INFERRED.

How the London work splits

From the bios and postings, EMEA KCS divides four ways [S140, S141, S150-S157] CONFIRMED (the framing is INFERRED):

  1. By region. Each senior RM owns a geography: UK, DACH, France/Benelux/Southern Europe, Nordics, Middle East, Central and Eastern Europe. Iberia is covered from Paris; no Madrid KCS bio exists [S149].
  2. By channel. Institutional (pensions, sovereigns, insurers, consultants), Family Capital (single-family offices), and Global Wealth Solutions (private banks and wealth platforms).
  3. By product. Private equity (including the evergreen K-PRIME and K-PEC), infrastructure, real estate, and credit (mostly Dublin).
  4. Support. CAPS for RFPs and DDQs; the new London analyst role for "investor reporting, fundraising support, KYC and investment onboarding" [S140].

Two signals point to growth in Europe. Four of the seven new KCS Managing Directors for 2026 are EMEA-based: Alice Bush and Daniel Valladares in London, Patricia Bandeira Vieira and Michael de Freitas in the Middle East [S165] CONFIRMED. And KKR is "increasingly localizing" in Europe, said the co-heads of KKR EMEA, Mattia Caprioli and Tara Davies, when announcing Milan [S168] CONFIRMED. The closest European intern analogue, a 2027 KCS off-cycle intern in Frankfurt, supports "the DACH Institutional and Family Capital teams" and coordinates "responses to client due diligence requests/RFPs, including underlying portfolio statistics, marketing materials and presentation decks" [S141] CONFIRMED.

Source uncertain

KKR does not publish reporting lines, so who reports to whom in London is inferred. The directory excludes Analysts and Associates, so the London junior count is an estimate. Bios can lag moves (for example, an infrastructure Partner still listed in London is moving to lead Milan [S149]). Peer London IR team sizes were not found, so no benchmark is given [S149] (gap).

Say this in the interview

"From the outside, London KCS looks like four groups: institutional and family capital relationship managers, consultant relations, Global Wealth Solutions under Markus Egloff, and a product team where infrastructure is the biggest cluster. I would expect an intern to support the relationship managers and one product team, and I would love to know which this summer." [S149, S150, S157]

Don't say this

"I want to work for [named MD] on her team." You do not know the reporting lines and neither does any public source. Say what work interests you (for example, family capital, or evergreen products for UK wealth managers) and let them map it to people.

Ten facts to carry into the room@@k3-takeaways@@

@@k4@@
Part 4

The role decoded, line by line

Every sentence KKR has written about KCS and its interns, translated into what you would actually do, who you would deal with, what good looks like and what it reveals about the firm.

How to read this part@@k4-how@@

KKR's KCS team description has eight lines. The internship programme adds four duty lines that apply to every team. Below, each of the twelve gets the same decoding block: what it means day to day, who the counterparties are, the tools, what good looks like, and the structural fact about KKR it reveals. Where the block is reasoning rather than a quoted fact, it is tagged INFERRED. The figure below is the map.

The eight lines of the KCS description@@k4-lines@@

Line 1. "consists of experienced professionals with diverse backgrounds dedicated to developing and servicing KKR's global network of investors and clients"
Day to day"Developing" means new clients and new money; "servicing" means reporting, meetings and answers for existing clients. The London analyst posting lists both: "Supporting Relationship Managers in fundraising activities" and "Ongoing servicing of existing clients" [S101] CONFIRMED.
CounterpartiesPension CIOs, sovereign fund teams, family office principals, private bank product heads, advisers [S70, S84] CONFIRMED.
ToolsCRM: a KKR wealth posting asks for "Proficiency in CRM systems (Salesforce)" and "meeting/call notes in CRM" [S103] CONFIRMED.
Good looks likeClients come back for the next fund and add strategies INFERRED.
Reveals about KKR"Diverse backgrounds" is literal: senior KCS people came from PIMCO, Goldman Sachs, UBS, Blackstone, Morgan Stanley, Citi, HSBC and from KKR's own investing and capital markets teams [S79, S120, S122, S123, S124, S129, S137] CONFIRMED. KKR hires laterally into KCS for specialist knowledge (wealth, insurance, a region) INFERRED.
Line 2. "Relationship managers in direct outreach to clients"
Day to dayRMs own a territory or a client list. They set meetings, run roadshows, pitch, negotiate and close. In EMEA the territories are UK, DACH, France/Benelux/Southern Europe, Nordics and Middle East [S150, S153, S154, S155, S151] CONFIRMED.
CounterpartiesClients directly, plus the consultants who advise them (a separate consultant relations team covers those) [S132, S135] CONFIRMED.
ToolsCRM, pitch books, roadshow schedules, pipeline trackers. The Frankfurt intern will "Maintain information on the DACH budgets and pipeline" [S141] CONFIRMED.
Good looks likeCapital raised, meetings held, pipeline converted, and trust: KKR's 10-K lists "duration of relationships" and "quality of services" among the bases of fundraising competition [S70] CONFIRMED.
Reveals about KKR"Direct" means KKR mostly covers clients with its own people rather than relying on placement agents INFERRED. The localisation push (Abu Dhabi 2025, Milan 2026) puts more RMs on the ground [S184, S168] CONFIRMED.
Line 3. "Product specialists providing specific support and expertise"
Day to dayEach specialist knows one asset class deeply. A Dublin credit posting says the team is "responsible for owning marketing materials, developing thought leadership and leading investor diligence processes" and will "Create and update content for client updates presentations, marketing decks and new business proposals" [S106] CONFIRMED.
CounterpartiesRMs (internal clients), investment teams and portfolio managers, and clients' due diligence teams [S106] CONFIRMED.
ToolsPitch decks, DDQ library, data rooms, performance data.
Good looks likeFast, accurate diligence answers and a clear story about the strategy INFERRED.
Reveals about KKRWith 24 strategies by 2020 [S94], no RM can know them all; specialists make breadth sellable. Credit alone has "over 30 product strategists" [S106] CONFIRMED.
Line 4. "Junior resources serving in a generalist capacity"
Day to dayThis is your line. Interns and analysts support several RMs and several products. Singapore intern tasks: "preparing client briefing materials, supporting meeting and roadshow logistics, maintaining CRM data, conducting market and client research, and assisting with sales territory management" [S107] CONFIRMED. Frankfurt: "Learn the platform, products and investment strategies across asset classes" [S141] CONFIRMED.

Good looks likeNothing goes out wrong. Fast turnaround. The RM never has to check your numbers INFERRED. Frankfurt asks for a "Strong support mindset" [S141] CONFIRMED.
Reveals about KKRGeneralist juniors see the whole shelf, which is the best way to learn a multi-strategy firm in a summer INFERRED.
Say this in the interview

"I read 'junior resources in a generalist capacity' as the most useful seat for learning, because the intern touches every product and every internal team. The London analyst posting lists seven internal teams you work with just to answer client requests." [S101]

Line 5. "Relationship-focused, solutions-oriented approach, able to deliver customized products"
Day to dayStart from the client's problem, not the fund that is raising. For a big pension that might be a separately managed account; for a family office a co-investment; for an insurer a "fully integrated balance sheet solution" [S84, S104] CONFIRMED.
CounterpartiesLarge institutions, insurers, family offices; internally product strategy and legal.
ToolsBespoke proposals; KKR's Total Portfolio Approach framing, "zero-based budgeting for portfolio construction" [S90] CONFIRMED.

Day to dayMatch each client to the right product: a drawdown fund, a K-Series fund, co-investment, KCM financing for a family's company, an insurance solution [S70, S84] CONFIRMED.
CounterpartiesClients and product teams.
ToolsThe product shelf; the client's profile and holdings in CRM.

Reveals about KKR"Services" is a real word: family offices are offered "Comprehensive Debt Solutions ... including buyouts and acquisition financings" [S84] CONFIRMED, which is a capital markets product sold through a KCS relationship.

CounterpartiesInvestment teams, the Global Macro team, senior leadership, other regions.
ToolsInternal networks; KKR Insights research.

The four intern duty lines@@k4-intern@@

Where these lines come from

Every duty and qualification line here is quoted from KKR's own 2027 London internship description, as published on the SEO London listing and the attached team descriptions [Advert]. The core sentence reads: "summer interns will be involved in helping identify attractive investment themes and opportunities, synthesizing industry and market data and analysing potential investments. Interns are encouraged to leverage KKR's approved AI tools to accelerate their work, deepen their learning, and contribute fresh perspectives on how emerging technology can enhance the way we operate." The SEO application form itself sits behind a login and was not read [S392].

Line 9. Identify investment themes
In KCS termsNot finding deals, but finding the stories clients want to hear and checking KKR has a product for each. Example themes in KKR's own 2026 output: infrastructure for AI and power demand, the Total Portfolio Approach, asset-based finance [S334, S90, S332] CONFIRMED.
CounterpartiesRMs, product specialists, KKR Insights and macro research.
Good looks likeA theme with evidence, a client type it suits and a KKR product it maps to INFERRED.
RevealsKCS sells views as well as funds. A KKR recruiter said the firm wants candidates who "understand how the macro environment is affecting investors and what that might mean for KKR's businesses" [S393] REPORTED.
Line 10. Synthesise industry and market data
In KCS termsTurn fundraising data, peer moves and client news into a one-page brief. Singapore interns do "market and client research" and "Support the production and maintenance of Institutional and Family Capital business metrics and reporting" [S107] CONFIRMED.
Good looks likeShort, sourced, so-what first. For example: "Q1 2026 private credit redemption requests topped $20bn industry-wide; here is what our wealth clients are asking" [S337] REPORTED.
RevealsThe analyst posting asks for the "ability to read information/situations from varying perspectives and tailor messages to suit different audiences" [S388] CONFIRMED.
Line 11. Analyse potential investments
In KCS termsLook at investments from the client's side: what a fund or co-investment adds to a client portfolio, its fees, liquidity, risk and track record. For a K-Series fund that means the 1.25% management fee and limited redemption terms [S111, S70] CONFIRMED. For a co-investment it means a fast read of the deal for a client INFERRED.
Good looks likeYou can say who the product is for and who it is not for INFERRED.
RevealsKCS people must understand the investing as well as the investors; several moved between investing, KCM and KCS [S129, S130, S137] CONFIRMED.
Line 12. "encouraged to leverage KKR's approved AI tools"
In KCS termsDraft first versions of DDQ answers, summarise long reports, tidy meeting notes, build first-pass slides. The London analyst posting asks for "Strong working knowledge of AI-enabled productivity tools, with the ability to use generative AI effectively and responsibly" [S101] CONFIRMED.
Good looks likeFaster drafts, every number and claim checked against the source, nothing confidential pasted into an unapproved tool INFERRED.
Reveals"Approved" is the key word: client data and fund numbers are confidential and regulated, so only sanctioned tools are allowed INFERRED.
Say this in the interview

"I would use the approved AI tools for first drafts and summaries, then check every figure against the official source myself, because in client work a DDQ answer or a performance number is a representation to the client." [S101, S70]

The London analyst posting, decoded@@k4-posting@@

On 7 October 2026 KKR advertised an EMEA Institutional Client Relations Analyst in London, for "up to 2 years" of experience [S101, S140] CONFIRMED. It is the closest public description of what the London team's juniors do. Every duty, verbatim [S101], with a decode:

Verbatim dutyWhat it means in practice (inferred unless tagged)
"a member of the fundraising support and investor relations team for KKR's EMEA based institutional & family capital clients"Two channels (institutions and families), one region. Not the wealth channel, which sits with GWS under Markus Egloff [S157] CONFIRMED.
"develop both client relationships and product expertise in a variety of different asset classes, including private equity, infrastructure, real estate, private and liquid credit strategies"Generalist across the whole shelf. "Liquid credit" means tradable loans and bonds, as opposed to private loans.
"work closely with Relationship Managers across EMEA, providing support for client investments with KKR"You are the RMs' engine room: packs, numbers, follow-ups.
"Managing a variety of reporting requirements for investors"Clients ask for data in their own formats (fees, holdings, ESG data, look-throughs). You compile, check and send.
"Supporting Relationship Managers in fundraising activities"Pitch books, meeting briefings, roadshow logistics, pipeline tracking.
"Partnering with clients to help with KYC & investment onboarding"Know-your-client checks (identity, ownership, source of funds, sanctions) and subscription paperwork before money can come in. Anti-money laundering rules apply [S70] CONFIRMED.
"Collaborating with various internal divisions globally to answer client requests (Product teams, Investment teams, Operations, Finance, Legal, Compliance, Risk)"Finding the person who knows the answer, getting it right and on time. This is where you learn the firm.
"Ongoing servicing of existing clients including delivering investment updates in meetings"Juniors present too, not just take notes. Prepare to speak about a portfolio clearly.
"Regular involvement in event coordination, team budgeting and business planning"Client events, AGMs, the team's own budget and targets.
Competencies: "Technical and aesthetic mastery of PowerPoint and Excel"; "Maturity, presence, sound judgment, and ability to form and express opinions"; "Additional language fluencies, particularly German or French, a plus"Slides must look KKR-quality. Opinions are wanted, so have some. German and French match the DACH and France/Benelux coverage [S153, S154] CONFIRMED.
Why this matters

The posting shows the job is half service, half sales. If you only talk about "pitching funds" you will sound like you have not read it. Mention reporting, KYC and answering client requests, and you will sound like you already work there.

A worked day: KCS summer intern in London@@k4-day@@

This is an illustrative day built only from the duties in KKR's KCS postings [S101, S107, S141]. It is not a reported account. The 2027 London programme runs from 6 June to 29 July 2027 (from the brief). Expect variety: no two days look alike INFERRED.

The life of a fundraise@@k4-fundraise@@

A flagship fund is a multi-year project for KCS. The diagram shows the stages from design to the next fund, with what KCS does at each. The sequence is the standard private markets pattern INFERRED; the examples are KKR's.

Key terms

Close: a date on which investors sign up and become bound. Side letter: a private agreement giving one investor extra terms (reporting, fee or legal points). Capital call: KKR asking investors to send part of their commitment. Distribution: cash paid back to investors. Re-up: an existing investor committing to the successor fund. Donnenfeld on GII V: "strong support from both longstanding clients who have partnered with us across multiple fund vintages and new investors" [S334] CONFIRMED.

The life of an RFP or DDQ@@k4-rfp@@

A request for proposal (RFP, called a "tender" in the UK and EU) asks managers to bid for a mandate. A due diligence questionnaire (DDQ) is a long list of questions an investor asks before committing: strategy, team, track record, risk, legal, operations, ESG, fees. KKR's Dublin posting: "Work with the internal CAPS team to complete tenders/Due Diligence Questionnaires for potential new clients across credit while leading investor diligence processes" [S106] CONFIRMED. Frankfurt interns "Coordinate responses to client due diligence requests/RFPs, including underlying portfolio statistics, marketing materials and presentation decks" [S141] CONFIRMED.

Your opinion goes here

Where would AI help most and where is it riskiest? A defensible view: most help in step 3 (finding and adapting past answers), most risk in step 6 (numbers), where a human must tie every figure to the official source. Add your own example of checking someone else's numbers.

The life of a co-investment syndication with KCM@@k4-coinvest@@

KKR's 10-K describes the mechanism. KKR Capital Markets "provides syndication services for co-investments in transactions participated in by KKR, our investment vehicles, Global Atlantic, and third-party clients, which may entitle the firm to receive transaction fees, management fees, and a carried interest" [S70] CONFIRMED. KKR may commit to more of a deal than it keeps and "syndicate a portion of our capital commitment to third parties. However, if we are unable to syndicate all or part of such commitment, or if such co-investors fail to fund their commitments, we may be required to fund the remaining commitment" [S70] CONFIRMED.

Key terms

Syndication: selling slices of a deal to other investors. Underwrite: commit to the whole amount first, taking the risk of not selling it. Wall-crossing: formally giving someone confidential (possibly price-sensitive) information, after which they are restricted from trading on it. MNPI: material non-public information.

Two channels compared: institutional vs private wealth@@k4-channels@@

The London analyst role covers institutions and family capital [S101]; wealth sits in GWS [S157]. But a summer intern may see both, and the work differs in shape. Institutions are reached directly, one large client at a time. Wealth is "business to business to consumer": KCS sells to a platform, the platform's advisers sell to individuals INFERRED.

DimensionInstitutional (and family capital)Private wealth (GWS)
Who you persuadeA CIO, an investment team, a consultant, a committeeA platform's due diligence team, then thousands of advisers
Main productsDrawdown funds, SMAs, co-investment [S70]K-Series evergreen funds, interval funds, feeders [S70, S92, S114]
MinimumsLarge single commitments (e.g. CalPERS $600m to NA XIII [S117])US K-Series aimed at accredited investors, $1m+ net worth [S76]; Capital Group KKR funds $1,000 minimum [S210]
Liquidity talkLong lock-up accepted; capital calls and distributionsLimited, periodic redemptions; must be explained before sale [S70, S338]
Regulation emphasisProfessional-investor marketing; AIFMD and UK private placement [S70]Suitability and investor protection: MiFID II, ELTIF Regulation in the EEA [S70]; US licences such as Series 7 [S103]
Junior workReporting, KYC, DDQs, meeting packs [S101]Outbound calls, territory and pipeline data, roadshows with platforms [S103]; adviser education material INFERRED
ScoreboardCommitments, re-ups, strategies per client INFERREDNet flows, platforms signed, redemptions [S76, S77]

The taxonomy of KCS activities and formats@@k4-taxonomy@@

Every activity in KCS sits somewhere on two axes: is it one-to-one or one-to-many, and is it about winning new money or keeping and growing existing money? Knowing the formats by name makes you sound like an insider.

FormatWhat it is, in one line
RoadshowA run of client meetings in one region over a few days, often around a fund launch.
AGMA fund's annual meeting for its investors: performance, portfolio, outlook, Q&A with senior investors.
Quarterly letter / reportThe regular update on fund value, cash flows and portfolio companies.
Data roomA secure online folder of fund documents for investors doing diligence.
Consultant reviewAn investment consultant's assessment and rating of a strategy, which many pension clients rely on.
Side letterA private agreement with one investor adding to the main fund terms.
WebinarOne-to-many online briefing, common in the wealth channel.
Platform due diligenceThe review a private bank or wirehouse runs before putting a KKR fund on its shelf for advisers.

Don't say this

"KCS is basically sales." It is partly sales, but the postings put reporting, KYC, client requests and investor diligence first [S101, S106]. Also avoid "KCS is the back office": the team "leads fundraising activities" [S106] and sits on KKR's main growth line.

The compliance dimension: bright lines@@k4-compliance@@

Client work at an asset manager is regulated work. KKR's 10-K names the frameworks: in the UK and EU it markets under "private placement exemptions and marketing registrations, for example under the AIFMD in Europe, the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 ... and the Alternative Investment Fund Managers Regulations 2013" [S70] CONFIRMED. Sales to EEA individuals are governed by MiFID II, AIFMD and the ELTIF Regulation, which "contain requirements for, among other things, marketing, investor suitability assessments, and conflicts of interest management" [S70] CONFIRMED. KKR's London LLPs are FCA-authorised [S171, S172] CONFIRMED.

Bright lineWhat it means for a juniorWhat to say unprompted
Marketing rulesOnly approved materials go to clients. Content is gated by investor type: KKR's wealth site is "only intended and directed to Institutional, Professional or Accredited Investors" [S83] CONFIRMED. No ad hoc spreadsheets of performance sent from your inbox INFERRED."I'd assume nothing goes to a client unless it's been through compliance, and I'd ask before sending anything new."
MNPI walls with KCMKCM handles financings and securities; co-investment involves confidential deal information. Wall-crossing and insider lists apply; never share deal details with an un-crossed client or colleague INFERRED. Product strategy head Amy Lesch sits on the Global Conflicts and Compliance Committee [S121] CONFIRMED."Working near Capital Markets, I'd expect strict information barriers and would treat any deal information as need-to-know."
Gifts, hospitality, briberyClient events and dinners are part of the job, so gifts and entertainment are logged and limited; public pension and sovereign clients raise anti-bribery sensitivity INFERRED. The 10-K warns "Financial crime laws may limit our investment and capital raising activities" [S70] CONFIRMED."Client entertainment is a tool, not a perk; I'd follow the logging rules."
Accuracy of numbersDDQ answers, returns and fees become representations to clients; errors are legal and regulatory risk INFERRED. Tie every figure to the official source."In this job a wrong number is worse than a late number."
KYC and AMLOnboarding is a named analyst task [S101]. No money is accepted until checks are complete INFERRED."KYC is the first thing that protects the firm, not paperwork."
AI tool useOnly "KKR's approved AI tools" (brief). Client names, holdings and unpublished performance never go into public tools; outputs are checked like any draft INFERRED. The posting asks for using generative AI "effectively and responsibly" [S101] CONFIRMED."I'd use AI for speed on drafts and never for the final check."
Why this matters

KKR's culture line is "our word is our bond", and Kravis tells of apologising to a bank's CEO after an employee retraded a deal in KKR's favour [S384] CONFIRMED. In KCS that culture shows up as accuracy and honesty with clients. Raising compliance yourself, briefly and calmly, signals you understand the seat.

Career path from the seat@@k4-career@@

The title ladder in KKR's directory and postings is Analyst, Associate (some postings say AVP), Principal, Director, Managing Director, Partner [S80, S101, S102, S104]. The titles are CONFIRMED; the order is INFERRED. Public bios show that people move across KCS, between KCS and Capital Markets, and from investing into KCS.

Pay data points for orientation only: a New York GWS internal sales analyst/associate role was advertised at $130,000 to $165,000 base [S103] and a Global Insurance Client Solutions principal at $190,000 to $230,000 base [S104] CONFIRMED. No London KCS pay data was found.

Your opinion goes here

Why KCS over an investing seat, in your words. A strong structure: (1) you want breadth across the whole firm, which KCS gives by design [S141]; (2) you are energised by explaining things to people, which is the job [S388]; (3) the growth is in new channels like wealth and insurance, so the seat is where KKR is changing fastest [S71, S73]. Then one personal example.

Say this in the interview

"What draws me to KCS is that it is the one seat that sees the whole of KKR: every strategy, every client type, and Capital Markets too. The London analyst role lists reporting, KYC, client requests and investment updates, so I know it is a service job as much as a sales job, and I like that. Accuracy and trust are the product." [S101, S141]

Don't say this

"I see KCS as a way into private equity." Interviewers hear that as a lack of commitment, and no public bio shows a KCS-to-investing move [S80]. If asked about the future, talk about growing within client solutions or across product and coverage, which the bios do show [S126, S132].

@@k5@@
Part 5

How KCS stands out: the competitive research on the role

Ten rival client teams side by side, the seven design choices that separate them, what only KKR's client model can claim, and where it does not lead.

Every big private markets firm has a team like KCS. The job is the same everywhere: find investors, match them to products, look after them, and bring them back for the next fund. What differs is what sits behind the team: how big the firm is, what it owns, and how its people are paid. This part compares KCS with its ten closest peers so you can say, with evidence, what makes KKR's version different and where it is behind.

Key terms used in this part

AUM (assets under management): all the money a firm looks after. Fee-paying AUM (FPAUM): the part that actually pays a management fee; analysts value this more. Firms use slightly different names (fee-earning, fee-generating, fee-bearing) for the same idea. Inflows / capital raised: new money clients committed in a period. Evergreen fund: a fund with no end date that takes new money monthly and lets investors ask for some back each quarter; the main product sold to wealthy individuals. Insurance affiliate: an insurance company owned by, or closely tied to, the asset manager, whose savings it invests.

Why this matters

KKR is a top-five firm but not the biggest, and in Q2 2026 it raised less than Brookfield, Blackstone, Apollo and Ares. The interesting story is not size. It is that KKR's money is spread across more kinds of "engine" than almost anyone else's, which changes what its client team can offer. INFERRED

Several cells are "not disclosed" or "not checked" because the research ran out of search budget. Never fill those gaps in an interview with guesses. If asked about, say, TPG's client team, say what you know (it was set up in 2020 to absorb the old fundraising team [S231]) and stop.

Wealth: where KKR is a fast follower@@k5-wealth@@

Private wealth means selling to individuals (usually rich ones, through banks and advisers) rather than to pension funds. It is the fastest-growing client channel in the industry and the place where the gap between KKR and the leader is widest.

KKR's position

  • K-Series rose from $25bn to $42bn in the year to June 2026 [S200] CONFIRMED. Management said wealth AUM grew "6x" in two and a half years [S207] CONFIRMED.
  • About 85% of K-Series is in private equity and infrastructure [S207] REPORTED. Blackstone's biggest wealth funds are in real estate and credit (BREIT, BCRED) [S213].
  • KKR has an "Exclusive Strategic Partnership" with Capital Group, a giant traditional fund manager, to sell public-plus-private funds with a $1,000 minimum [S210] CONFIRMED.
  • KKR runs "KKR Academies" for about 100 advisers at a time [S207] CONFIRMED.

The industry backdrop

  • Partners Group: $4.2bn of evergreen demand in H1 2026 but $3.8bn of redemptions, so net flows were "only modestly positive" [S239] CONFIRMED.
  • Blue Owl's private wealth new money fell to $1.7bn in Q2 from $4.4bn a year earlier [S234] REPORTED.
  • CVC grew wealth 4x in a year to €6.7bn, from a small base [S238] CONFIRMED.
  • KKR said its wealth flows were still up 20% net year to date [S207] REPORTED.
Your opinion goes here

A view you could defend: "KKR is a fast follower in wealth. Its edge is not scale, where Blackstone is about eight times bigger, but product mix (private equity and infrastructure evergreen funds) and a distribution route through Capital Group's adviser network that no rival has." Label it as your view. [S200, S207, S210, S215] INFERRED

Size against staffing@@k5-staffing@@

A crude test of efficiency is AUM per employee: how much money each person looks after. It is crude because firms that own insurers also employ insurance staff (actuaries, policy administrators), which pulls the ratio down.

Two readings matter for KCS. First, KKR's CFO says the firm can grow "without requiring us to significantly increase our headcount or sacrifice our culture" [S207] CONFIRMED. Second, KKR's client team of about 320 looks after a firm of $796bn, while Blackstone has 357 people in wealth alone plus a separate institutional team [S106, S215] REPORTED. So each KCS person covers a wide product shelf. For an intern, that means exposure to many products at once. INFERRED

Every firm in this group has funds, credit, some wealth product and some insurance link. They differ in how they built those pieces. These are the points where the research found no rival that can say the same thing. Each is worded so you do not overclaim. "Only" here means "no peer in this research set", not "nobody in the world".

Claim 1. One client team selling four engines that KKR owns or runsSTRONG

@@k6@@
Part 6

The fundraising industry and its regulation

How capital is raised, who helps, what investors check, and the rules that bind every conversation with a client.

Why the client function has its own industry@@r-why@@

Private markets firms do two jobs. They invest money, and they raise it. This part is about the second job: the people, steps and rules that sit between an investor's savings and a fund like KKR's. It is the ground a Global Client Solutions (KCS) intern stands on every day.

The basics section explained the fund itself: a general partner (GP, the manager) and limited partners (LPs, the investors) signing a limited partnership agreement (LPA). Here we look at how an LP is found, convinced and kept, and at the walls of regulation that decide what may be said, to whom, and where.

$1.3tn
Private capital raised in 2025, about flat on 2024 (Bain) [S262] CONFIRMED
78.2%
Share of capital going to funds above $1bn, H1 2026 (59.1% in 2021) [S260] CONFIRMED
7,739
Private equity funds on the road chasing LPs, Q2 2026 (Preqin) [S266] CONFIRMED

Read those three numbers together. The pot of money is not growing. More funds than at any time in five years are competing for it. And the biggest managers take a rising share. In a market like that, the quality of a firm's client team decides who wins INFERRED.

A short history of raising money@@r-history@@

1980s to 1990s: the address book. GPs raised money mostly through their partners' personal networks. A fund was a handful of relationships with pension funds and wealthy families INFERRED.

2000s to 2010s: the professional IR team. As funds grew to tens of billions and LPs multiplied, the large GPs built in-house investor relations (IR) or "client solutions" teams. These have relationship managers per region or client type, product specialists per strategy, and junior generalists INFERRED. KKR's own team, KCS, was "first formed in 2009" and now has "over 300 executives located in over 20 [cities] across four continents" [S390] CONFIRMED. It is organised around "Sales/Relationship Management and Product/Strategy Management" [S390] CONFIRMED.

2010s: the LP pushes back. LPs organised. The Institutional Limited Partners Association (ILPA) published its first Principles in September 2009 and its first due diligence questionnaire in 2013 [S317, S320] CONFIRMED. Fund terms, reporting and diligence became more standard.

2020s: the individual arrives. Bain estimates individuals hold about 50% of global assets ($275tn to $295tn) but only 16% of the assets held in alternative funds [S293] REPORTED. Closing that gap is the "democratisation" story. Platforms such as iCapital and CAIS, plus wirehouses and private banks, now carry private funds to wealthy individuals. PitchBook says "growing inflows from retail investors are becoming the main source of new capital" for private equity [S260] CONFIRMED.

Why this matters

KKR's 10-Q says traditional private equity was over 70% of its assets in 2010 and is "less than 25%" today [S332] CONFIRMED. The client function grew up alongside that shift: more products, more client types, more rules. A KCS junior now explains credit, infrastructure, insurance-backed strategies and wealth funds, not one buyout fund.

The players: who stands between savings and a fund@@r-players@@

The map below shows the cast. Two flows matter. Money moves along the solid lines. Advice, introductions, rules and standards move along the dashed lines. The GP's client team sits in the middle of both.

PlayerWhat they do, in plain EnglishExamples and facts
GP client teamFinds, wins and keeps investors. Answers every question after the money arrives.KKR KCS: relationship managers, product specialists, junior generalists (official team text). Works "in partnership with Capital Markets in the syndication/distribution of product".
Placement agentAn outside firm hired by a GP to raise money, often for mid-sized or first-time managers, or to reach new LP types.Evercore, Campbell Lutyens, Park Hill (PJT), Lazard, Rede, Asante. PEI's ranking to May 2024 covered 38 agents raising $41bn of "new" capital [S322] REPORTED. Typical success fee around 2% to 2.5% of capital raised (indicative only) [S322] REPORTED.
Investment consultant / gatekeeperAdvises an LP on which funds to back. Often the first screen a fund must pass.Cambridge Associates, Mercer, Aon, Hamilton Lane, StepStone (the last two also invest directly) INFERRED.
Feeder platformLets a wealth adviser put many clients into one "feeder" fund that invests in the GP's fund. Handles paperwork, minimums, reporting.iCapital (founded 2013) raised $820m in July 2025 at a reported $7.5bn valuation [S321] REPORTED. CAIS.
Wirehouse / private bankLarge brokerages and banks whose advisers sell funds to wealthy clients.Morgan Stanley, Merrill, UBS, Wells Fargo INFERRED.
ILPAThe LPs' trade body. Writes best-practice terms and standard templates.Offices in Toronto, Washington DC and London [S317] CONFIRMED.
Key terms

Gatekeeper: anyone who controls access to an LP's money, usually a consultant. Feeder fund: a small fund whose only job is to pool many investors and invest in one bigger fund. Re-up: an existing LP committing to the manager's next fund. Re-ups are the cheapest money a client team ever raises INFERRED.

How an institutional LP picks a manager@@r-funnel@@

A pension fund does not wire $200m after one good meeting. Selection takes months and passes through a funnel of checks (see the funnel figure). Each stage creates work for the GP's client team. The KKR EMEA client relations analyst advert lists exactly this work: "investor reporting", "supporting relationship managers in fundraising", "KYC and onboarding", and answering requests with product, investment, operations, finance, legal, compliance and risk teams [S388] CONFIRMED.

The stages in words

  1. Screening. The LP or its consultant filters by track record, strategy fit and team stability INFERRED.
  2. Investment due diligence. Deal-by-deal attribution (which deals made the money), DPI (cash actually returned divided by cash paid in), PME (a comparison with a stock index), and reference calls INFERRED.
  3. Due diligence questionnaire (DDQ). A long standard form, often the ILPA DDQ. The first ILPA DDQ came out in 2013, was updated in 2016 and 2018, and DDQ 2.0 arrived in November 2021 with new sections on succession planning, co-investment, GP-led secondaries, credit facilities and cybersecurity [S320] REPORTED.
  4. Operational due diligence (ODD). A separate team checks the back office: valuation policy, cyber, compliance, administrator, auditor. The FCA's March 2025 review of private market valuations found weaknesses in governance records, conflicts, independence and ad hoc revaluations [S310] REPORTED. Expect ODD teams to ask about exactly those.
  5. Investment committee. The LP's own board or committee approves INFERRED.
  6. Legal. LPA terms and a side letter: a private contract giving one LP extra terms such as fee breaks, reporting rights, co-investment rights or the right to skip certain deals. A most-favoured-nation (MFN) clause lets an LP claim terms given to similar or smaller LPs INFERRED.
  7. Commitment and monitoring. Quarterly reports, annual meetings, a seat on the LP advisory committee (LPAC) for big LPs, and in time the next re-up INFERRED.

ILPA: the rule book written by the clients@@r-ilpa@@

ILPA's three guiding principles are alignment of interest, governance and transparency, which it says "form the essence of an effective private equity partnership" [S317] CONFIRMED. ILPA has no legal power. Its weight comes from the fact that its members are the LPs.

What LPs value in 2026@@r-lpvalues@@

~14%
Distributions as a share of NAV in 2025; below 15% for four years running (Bain) [S262] CONFIRMED

  • Cash back (DPI). Exits have been slow, so LPs are short of distributions. This is the most-watched number in every meeting [S262] CONFIRMED.
  • A clear, repeatable strategy. Bain: "Investors more than ever are focused on funds that have a clear, repeatable, and easily explained strategy" [S262] CONFIRMED. This is a communication skill as much as an investment one.
  • Co-investment (investing directly next to the fund, usually at low or no fee) [S260] CONFIRMED.
  • Fewer, bigger relationships. PitchBook notes "ongoing consolidation of LP relationships" [S260] REPORTED.
  • Standard reporting. The ILPA templates [S318] CONFIRMED.
  • ESG and diversity data, built into ILPA DDQ 2.0 [S320] but politically contested in the US in 2025 to 2026 INFERRED.

Regulation in one picture: who may be marketed what@@r-map@@

All fundraising rules answer one question: who is this investor, and where are they? Professional investors are assumed to look after themselves. Ordinary savers are protected, so they can only buy private assets through special, regulated products. The map below is the one to carry into an interview.

The European Union@@r-eu@@

AIFMD: the base law

The Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive (AIFMD), Directive 2011/61/EU, regulates managers of "alternative" funds: private equity, credit, real estate and hedge funds. It was signed on 8 June 2011, entered into force on 21 July 2011 (some sources say 22 July), and had to be in national law by 22 July 2013 [S300] CONFIRMED.

  • Marketing passport. From 22 July 2013 an EU manager could sell an EU fund to professional investors across the EU after a notification [S300] CONFIRMED.
  • NPPR (national private placement regime). Non-EU managers have no passport. They use each country's own private placement rules under Article 42, country by country [S300] CONFIRMED.

Pre-marketing and reverse solicitation

The Cross-Border Distribution package (Directive (EU) 2019/1160 and Regulation (EU) 2019/1156) was published on 12 July 2019, came into force on 1 August 2019 and applied from 2 August 2021 [S299] CONFIRMED. It defined pre-marketing: testing investor interest before a fund is set up or notified, without an offer. An EU manager must tell its home regulator within two weeks of starting. AIMA's summary: "Within two weeks of starting to pre-market, an EU AIFM must send an informal letter or email to its home regulator" [S299] CONFIRMED.

Reverse solicitation means the investor approached the manager on its own initiative, so no "marketing" happened. The package closed the loophole: any subscription by a professional investor within 18 months of pre-marketing counts as marketing [S299] CONFIRMED. For a client team, this means every early conversation in Europe is logged and timed.

AIFMD II

Directive (EU) 2024/927 was published in the Official Journal on 26 March 2024, entered into force on 15 April 2024, and had to apply from 16 April 2026 [S296, S294] CONFIRMED. Linklaters marked the day: "AIFMD II takes effect at last" [S344] CONFIRMED.

ChangeDetailWhy a client team cares
Loan-originating fundsLeverage caps of 175% (open-ended) and 300% (closed-ended); 20% limit per financial borrower; keep 5% of each loan sold; no "originate-to-distribute"; closed-ended unless liquidity fits [S295, S297] CONFIRMEDShapes how European direct-lending funds are built and described
Liquidity management tools (LMTs)Open-ended funds must pick at least two from a list: gates, notice periods, redemption fees, swing pricing, and others [S295, S294] CONFIRMED. Commission adopted the LMT standards on 17 Nov 2025; ESMA guidelines published 12 Mar 2026 [S298] REPORTEDExplains to wealth clients why they cannot always exit when they want
DelegationMore reporting on delegation; at least two full-time EU-resident people running the business [S294] REPORTEDAffects where European fund entities sit
NPPR tighteningNon-EU managers and funds must not be in EU AML high-risk or tax non-cooperative lists [S294] REPORTEDFund domicile choice
GrandfatheringLoan funds set up before 15 Apr 2024 are exempt until 16 Apr 2029 [S297] CONFIRMEDOlder funds behave differently

Not every country was ready: Belgium, for example, had not published its law by the deadline [S294] REPORTED. New reporting starts on 16 April 2027, and the Commission said non-essential Level 2 detail would wait until after 1 October 2027 [S344, S298] CONFIRMED.

ELTIF 2.0 and MiFID II

The European Long-Term Investment Fund regulation, revised as Regulation (EU) 2023/606 ("ELTIF 2.0"), applies from 10 January 2024. It removed the €10,000 minimum for retail investors and widened eligible assets. Its technical standards became Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/2759, published on 25 October 2024 [S301, S302] CONFIRMED. Morningstar counts 189 new ELTIFs since the start of 2024; Scope counts a record 113 launches in 2025 and about €34bn of assets at end-2025, up 55% [S302] REPORTED.

MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU) has applied since 3 January 2018. Its product governance rules make manufacturers and distributors define a "target market" for each product, so a fund is only sold to the kind of client it was designed for INFERRED (dates not re-verified).

The United Kingdom@@r-uk@@

The UK AIFM regime and its rewrite

The UK put AIFMD into law in 2013 and kept it after Brexit. Overseas funds still reach UK investors through the UK NPPR [S304] REPORTED. HM Treasury and the FCA opened a reform consultation on 7 April 2025 [S304] CONFIRMED. Then came FCA CP26/28 "The UK AIFM Regime", published in July 2026 (14 July per Macfarlanes; Debevoise's note is dated 23 July) [S345, S303] CONFIRMED.

  • A new "ALTS" sourcebook. Investor disclosures become less prescriptive; firms choose how to disclose leverage [S303, S345] CONFIRMED.
  • UK managers marketing UK funds move from a 20-day pre-approval to a simple notification. NPPR kept with limited changes [S303] CONFIRMED.
  • Companion papers: CP26/27 on pay (the FCA "does not propose to make malus and clawback mandatory") and CP26/26 on reporting [S303] CONFIRMED.
  • Comments close on 14 October 2026, three days after this pack was written. Policy statement in 2027; rules in force 2028 [S303] CONFIRMED.

Retail and wealth routes in the UK

  • LTAF (Long-Term Asset Fund). Rules in force 15 November 2021. PS23/7 (29 June 2023) made LTAF units "Restricted Mass Market Investments" from 3 July 2023, opening them to retail investors with protections, and to self-select DC pensions and SIPPs [S305, S306] CONFIRMED.
  • Financial promotions exemptions. On 31 January 2024 the high-net-worth thresholds rose to £170,000 income or £430,000 net assets. After an industry backlash a new order from 27 March 2024 restored £100,000 and £250,000 and brought back the "two or more unlisted investments" test for self-certified sophisticated investors [S307] CONFIRMED. A good example of rules moving twice in two months.
  • Consumer Duty. Applied to open products from 31 July 2023 and closed products from 31 July 2024. It requires firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers [S308] CONFIRMED.
  • SMCR (Senior Managers and Certification Regime). Extended to FCA solo-regulated firms, which include most UK private markets managers, on 9 December 2019 (PS19/20) [S309] CONFIRMED. It makes named senior people personally accountable.

UK pensions: the Mansion House Accord and the Pension Schemes Act 2026

The Mansion House Accord (13 May 2025) is voluntary. 17 workplace pension providers, covering about 90% of active defined contribution (DC) savers, pledged to put at least 10% of DC default funds into private markets by 2030, with at least 5% in the UK. It could unlock up to £50bn, about £25bn in the UK [S315] CONFIRMED. HM Treasury: "At least 5 percent of these portfolios will be ringfenced for the UK" [S315] CONFIRMED.

The Pension Schemes Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 29 April 2026 after the Bill was introduced on 5 June 2025 [S316, S346] CONFIRMED. Main points:

  • Large multi-employer DC schemes need a default fund of at least £25bn by 2030 ("megafunds"); a transition route exists for schemes of £10bn or more that can reach £25bn by 2035 [S346] CONFIRMED.
  • A reserve power lets the government, once and not before 1 January 2028, require megafunds to hold "qualifying assets" (private equity, venture capital, private credit, land, infrastructure, unlisted shares). Cap: 10% of the default fund, of which no more than 5% UK-specific. Trustees can opt out if compliance is "likely not to be in the best interests of members". The power lapses at end-2032 if unused [S346] CONFIRMED.
  • Separately, the Local Government Pension Scheme (over £400bn across 86 funds in England and Wales) is consolidating from eight pools into six [S347] REPORTED.

The United States@@r-us@@

  • Regulation D. Rule 506(b) allows private offerings with no general solicitation (advertising). Rule 506(c), effective 23 September 2013 under the JOBS Act, allows general solicitation if every buyer is a verified accredited investor [S314] CONFIRMED.
  • Accredited investor. An individual with income over $200,000 ($300,000 joint) in each of the last two years, or net worth over $1m excluding the home [S314] CONFIRMED. August 2020 amendments added professional licence routes (Series 7, 65, 82) [S275] REPORTED. Around 30 September 2026 the SEC proposed a FINRA-developed accredited investor exam (pass valid ten years) plus Series 79, 86 and 87, CPA, CFA and CFP routes, with a 60-day comment period [S275] REPORTED. Chairman Paul Atkins: "accredited investor access to private offerings should not be limited solely to individuals satisfying financial thresholds" [S275] REPORTED.
  • Marketing Rule (Rule 206(4)-1). Adopted 22 December 2020, effective 4 May 2021, compliance from 4 November 2022. It replaced the old advertising and cash solicitation rules [S313] CONFIRMED. It governs how performance is shown in any pitch book.
  • Private Fund Adviser Rules. Adopted August 2023 (quarterly statements, audits, restricted activities, preferential treatment, adviser-led secondaries). Vacated in full by the Fifth Circuit on 5 June 2024 in National Association of Private Fund Managers v. SEC [S311, S312] CONFIRMED. Much of what they required now travels through ILPA templates and side letters instead INFERRED.
  • 401(k) access. Executive Order 14330, "Democratizing Access to Alternative Assets for 401(k) Investors", signed 7 August 2025 [S273] CONFIRMED. The Department of Labor proposed a process-based safe harbour on 30 March 2026, with six factors: performance, fees, liquidity, valuation, benchmarks and complexity. Comments closed 1 June 2026 [S272, S274, S342] CONFIRMED. No final rule found as of 11 October 2026 [S343] REPORTED.
  • SEC retail agenda. A roundtable on retail access to private investments on 4 March 2026 [S277] REPORTED; in early October 2026 the SEC reportedly voted to propose wider retail access through regulated funds [S368] REPORTED.

The regulation timeline, 2011 to 2028@@r-timeline@@

The walls around a client function@@r-walls@@

A client team talks to outsiders all day, and it sits inside a firm that holds secrets. Four kinds of wall keep the two apart (see the figure below). The detail differs by firm and is set by each firm's compliance team; what follows is the standard industry pattern, not KKR's internal policy INFERRED.

  • Information barrier (the "Chinese wall"). Separates people with MNPI from people who trade listed securities. Breaching it risks insider dealing INFERRED.
  • Need-to-know wall. A client team learns about live deals only when compliance approves it ("wall-crossing"). Example: before DCC confirmed an approach from Energy Capital Partners and KKR on 29 April 2026, any knowledge of the bid would have been MNPI about a London-listed company [S356] REPORTED. The application to KCS is INFERRED.
  • Marketing gate. Every pitch book, DDQ answer and performance figure is approved before it leaves. It must match the investor type and country (the "who may be marketed what" map), meet EU pre-marketing timing and the Marketing Rule in the US [S299, S313] CONFIRMED; how firms apply them is INFERRED.
  • Gifts and entertainment. Hospitality given or received is logged, kept within limits and pre-approved where policy requires; extra care applies to public pension officials INFERRED.
Why this matters

On governance, litigation and regulation, LP questionnaires want the approved answer. On the August 2026 DOJ settlement, KKR's public line is that the $250m civil penalty "will have no financial impact on the firm, our funds, or any of our investors and will be fully reimbursed by outside law firms" [S349] CONFIRMED. A junior repeats that line and nothing more.

What to say about all this@@r-say@@

What a candidate should be able to say unprompted

  1. "Fundraising is concentrating: funds above $1bn took 78.2% of capital in H1 2026, against 59.1% in 2021." [S260]
  2. "LPs choose through a funnel: consultant screen, due diligence, the ILPA DDQ, operational due diligence, investment committee, side letter, then commitment."
  3. "In Europe a non-EU manager markets through national private placement; AIFMD II applied from 16 April 2026." [S300, S294]
  4. "In the UK, CP26/28 proposes three tiers of manager by size, with new rules in 2028; the Pension Schemes Act 2026 caps any mandation at 10% private, 5% UK." [S303, S346]
  5. "In the US the direction is wider access: EO 14330 in August 2025, the DOL safe harbour proposal in March 2026, and the SEC's accredited investor proposal this autumn." [S273, S272, S275]
Say this in the interview

"Regulation is moving in two directions at once. Access is widening for individuals, through ELTIF 2.0, the LTAF and the US 401(k) work. But the rules on credit funds and liquidity are getting tighter, through AIFMD II. A client team has to sell the first while explaining the second."

Don't say this

"The Mansion House Accord forces UK pensions to invest 10% in private markets." It is voluntary. The legal backstop is a reserve power in the Pension Schemes Act 2026, capped at the same 10% / 5% levels and not usable before 1 January 2028 [S315, S346].

Say this in the interview

"The SEC's private fund adviser rules were vacated in June 2024, so a lot of LP protection now comes from ILPA's templates and from side letters. That puts more of the transparency burden on the client team."

Don't say this

"Reverse solicitation is an easy way round EU marketing rules." Since August 2021, a subscription within 18 months of pre-marketing counts as marketing [S299]. Calling it a loophole signals you would be a compliance risk.

What is happening right now

The stories from the last six months that a KCS interviewer will expect you to know, and what to say about each.

The six months in one paragraph@@n-summary@@

KKR is having a record year while parts of its industry wobble. That tension is the story an interviewer will want you to hold in your head.

KKR raised $34bn of new money in Q2 2026 and $133bn over the 12 months to 30 June, and manages $796bn [S330] CONFIRMED. Co-CEO Scott Nuttall said: "We expect a record fundraising year for the firm" [S362] REPORTED. Two flagship funds closed: North America Fund XIV at about $23bn in April and Global Infrastructure Investors V at $19.2bn in August [S335, S334] CONFIRMED. The private wealth funds (K-Series) reached $42bn [S330] CONFIRMED. Meanwhile wealthy individuals asked to pull more than $20bn out of private credit funds in Q1, and several managers, KKR among them, limited withdrawals [S337, S338] REPORTED. Regulators kept opening private markets to ordinary savers (US 401(k) proposal, SEC accredited investor proposal, UK Pension Schemes Act 2026) while rewriting fund-manager rules (AIFMD II, the new UK AIFM regime) [S342, S275, S346, S344, S345]. Inside KKR, the founders' special control rights end by 31 December 2026 at the latest, and KKR settled a $250m civil case with the US Department of Justice in August [S332, S349] CONFIRMED.

KKR's scoreboard in four charts@@n-numbers@@

For a client team, these are the numbers that matter most: how much KKR manages, how much it raised, and how fast the wealth channel grows. AUM (assets under management) is all the money KKR looks after. "New capital raised" is the money clients committed in the period: the direct output of KCS's work INFERRED.

Why this matters

The fastest-growing line is the wealth channel: K-Series AUM rose 68% in a year, from $25bn to $42bn [S330] CONFIRMED. From Q2 2026 KKR also reports K-Series private equity performance fees (about $160m in Q2) inside Fee Related Earnings, which makes wealth profits look more like steady fees [S332] CONFIRMED. Next results: 9 November 2026 [S333] REPORTED.

KKR's house view in plain English@@n-houseview@@

Henry McVey is KKR's Head of Global Macro and Asset Allocation and CIO of its Balance Sheet [S360] CONFIRMED. His team's outlooks are KKR's public "house view": what the firm thinks about the economy. Clients read them, and client teams use them in meetings INFERRED. KKR's head of talent acquisition told Fortune that KKR wants candidates who "understand how the macro environment is affecting investors" [S393] REPORTED. These two documents are how you show that.

Dec 2025: "Outlook for 2026: High Grading"

The economy is fine but the cycle is late. Do not run from risk; upgrade what you own, how it is financed and who you deal with, because upgrading is cheap today. "Using an education analogy, we think a B is an A in this environment, but a C could be an F." Calls include: create your own returns through operational improvement; favour firms that use AI to grow margins; "We want to own more Asia at this point in the cycle"; own "collateral-based cash flows" because inflation has a higher "resting heart rate" [S361] CONFIRMED.

Jun 2026: "The Divergence Conundrum"

"The cycle continues, but the rules of the game are changing." The economy moves from "a low-cost, efficiency-first model" to one where "redundancy, reliability, resilience, and control carry a higher premium". Some sectors attract capital (AI, productivity, national security); others struggle (housing, lower-income consumers, rate-sensitive sectors). "For investors, the implication is not to avoid risk, but to be more disciplined in how that risk is owned" [S360] CONFIRMED.

Other calls worth knowing from the mid-year update [S360] CONFIRMED: since ChatGPT launched, S&P 500 real revenue per worker is up about 8% after 20 years of no growth; goods inflation should settle about 100 basis points (1 percentage point) above pre-pandemic levels; stocks and bonds diversify each other less; in Europe KKR favours infrastructure, defence, grids, logistics and the periphery (Spain, Italy, Poland), not just a weak Germany; and manager selection "is a bigger part of returns" when results vary more between managers.

Say this in the interview

"KKR's mid-year outlook says the cycle continues but the rules are changing, and that manager selection matters more when returns diverge. That is a fundraising argument as much as a macro view: it explains why capital is concentrating in large platforms like KKR."
